## R90 — PAGE_SIZE IS 4096, NOT 16384. kalloc.2048 is N=2, so R89's index-0
## landing was a COIN FLIP. My own R89.3 refinement needs qualifying too.
## RECIPE L: first recipe where a QUIET BOOT is the success signal.

### R90.1 — Our kalloc.768 figure settled the page size, and it was 4096

R89.4 flagged that kalloc.768's chunk is 12,288 B / 16 elements and that
N = alloc_size/elem_size rather than pagesize/elem_size. The app-session took
that and decoded the `alloc_size` selection algorithm itself
(0xfffffff0076d02e4..0340, ZONE_MAX_ALLOC_SIZE = 0x8000, fragmentation-minimising
with ties keeping the smaller candidate, `zone+0xf8` = alloc_size). Running it:

    PAGE_SIZE   alloc_size(768)   N    matches our 12288/16 ?
    **4096**    **12288** (3 pg)  **16**   **YES, exactly**
    16384       16384    (1 pg)   21      no   (and 12288 isn't even a legal
                                               alloc_size at 16 KB pages)

**=> `page_shift = 12`. The project's inherited "16 KB pages" belief was wrong
for this kernel.** A hardware measurement beat an assumption, which is the right
way round. It also retires their §17.2 note-9 false-zero trap for `page_shift`.

**Consequence for R89.2**: kalloc.2048's alloc_size is 4096 = ONE page holding
**TWO** elements. So **N = 2, not 8**, and Recipe K's victim landing at chunk
index 0 was a **50% coin flip, not a 1-in-8 fluke**. Every "87.5% in
kalloc.2048" figure (theirs and mine in R88.2) is wrong; the right number is 50%.

Corrected usable (non-cached, N>=2) zones at 4 KiB pages:
    1664: alloc 28672 (7 pg) N=17 -> 94.1%   needs 16 groom objects
    1280: alloc 20480 (5 pg) N=16 -> 93.8%   needs 15
     768: alloc 12288 (3 pg) N=16 -> 93.8%   needs 15
    1152: alloc  8192 (2 pg) N=7  -> 85.7%   needs 6
     576: alloc  4096 (1 pg) N=7  -> 85.7%   needs 6
    6144: alloc 12288 (3 pg) N=2  -> 50.0%   needs 1
    2048: alloc  4096 (1 pg) N=2  -> 50.0%   needs 1
Also corrected on their side: **kalloc.576 and kalloc.768 are NOT per-CPU
cached** - the caching bitmap 0x27fff is indices 0-14 plus 17, i.e. {16..512} and
{1024} only. An over-broad reading of "16..512 and 1024" had been excluding them.

### R90.2 — My R89.3 refinement: correct, but only in a HIGH-N zone

I claimed that owning N-1 elements lets us choose which slot stays free, removing
the index-0 failure mode and taking 87.5% to ~100%. Their §25.3 walked back their
own 100% claim for the right reason, and it applies to mine: **at N=2 the chunk
parity is unobservable.** If the zone already has a partially-free chunk, our
first allocation tops it up next to a FOREIGN object and our second opens a fresh
one; which of those the victim ends up beside depends on zone state we cannot
see, and three boot jobs already allocate in kalloc.2048.
**So my refinement holds only where we own ALL N of a chunk - i.e. in a high-N
zone (768/1280/1664), where owning every element makes every mate ours and the
result is parity-independent.** At N=2 it is a coin flip either way. Qualifying
R89.3 accordingly rather than leaving the unconditional claim standing.
Their §25.1 did confirm the LIFO link itself from both ends on one field
(`free_to_zone` writes +0x10 at 0xfffffff0076d1520, `try_alloc_from_zone` reads
it at 0xfffffff0076d3050), so free-then-alloc does return the same element.
Their §25.4 adds a real hazard: any same-zone allocation between our free and
the victim steals the slot, so the free must be tightly timed - another argument
for the high-N zones, which have no boot jobs allocating into them.

### R90.3 — RECIPE L (job 685, armed, CHECKPOINT PASSED, 13,846 B)

Designed so that WINNING is provably harmless, which makes a quiet boot the
signal instead of an ambiguity:

    GPT bait   sectors 0-15 RAW, K's CRC-correct header (PLBA 64, nEnt 12,
               eSz 128), CRC 0x00779aea re-verified by me
    victim     dbr = 4 -> allocSize 2048 -> kalloc.2048 (N=2)
    table      runCount 36 -> 0xf4+40*36 = **1,684 B** inside a 2,048 B element
               -> **SLACK = 364 unused bytes** at that element's tail,
               and the table is live from attach to detach
    poison     zlib at sector 64, 3 sectors (1,536 < 2,048 strictly)
    **L = 2048 + 256 = 2304 -> dst = V - 256, so the write touches only the TOP
    256 BYTES of the neighbour, and 256 < 364.** If the neighbour is our table,
    every written byte lands in UNUSED SLACK of an object we own: zero damage.
    payload    size base 0x1C00, word3 tag 0x65XXXXXX - unique to this run
               (K used 0x1800, J 0x1000/0x1400, H/I a different field position)

    QUIET 7 MIN  -> **WE OWNED THE NEIGHBOUR.** First end-to-end proof that aim
                    works on hardware, and it needs no trust-cached binaries and
                    no groom objects beyond our own merged table.
    cookie panic -> neighbour was a FREE element (the R89 outcome)
    live-data panic with tag 0x65 -> neighbour was a foreign live object; the
                    ruler gives the offset
~50% per boot at N=2, and a loss now writes only 256 bytes, making this also the
least destructive recipe run so far. If it is quiet, re-run it unchanged once to
check the result is not a fluke (the R83 discipline).

## R91 — RECIPE L: 30 SECONDS OF UPTIME AND **NO KERNEL PANIC AT ALL**.
## Plus three infrastructure faults found the hard way, all now fixed or documented.

Recipe L (job 685) booted ~16:57. the author: "booted normally, played setup chime, and
after about 30 seconds it pop crashed and restarted, normally." He then pulled
power and went to DFU.

### R91.1 — The result: not a win, but the gentlest outcome yet, and NOT a panic

    30 s of uptime, past the setup chime  (Recipe K: crash-looped before the chime;
      J: ~2 crashes; H/I: seconds after the chime)
    **No PEEP record on ANY /dev/diskN -> the kernel wrote NO PANIC LOG.**

So Recipe L's 256-byte write did not kill the kernel. It survived 30 s and then
the machine restarted without a kernel panic - i.e. a userspace crash cascade or
a watchdog reset, not a kernel fault. That is consistent with a much smaller
write landing somewhere that took time to be consumed.

It is **not** the quiet-boot win condition (R90.3 required 7 clean minutes), so
we cannot claim the neighbour was our table. But it is the first boot where our
write landed and the KERNEL stayed alive, which is a real step: it means a
non-fatal write is reachable, which R86.3 had doubted.

### R91.2 — The previous panic was CLEARED, and that is a methodology rule

disk4 (the panic partition) returned 262,144 B with panic records for jobs
648-684, and returns **0 bytes** now. Nothing new was written and Recipe K's
panic is gone. The likely cause: Recipe L booted far enough (30 s, past the
chime) for **DumpPanic** - one of the 11 RunAtLoad root jobs - to run, consume
the panic region and clear it.
**RULE: pull the panic BEFORE the next cold boot. A boot that survives to
DumpPanic destroys the previous panic.** We happened to pull Recipe K's in time;
a slower turnaround would have silently lost it.

### R91.3 — FAULT 1: the panic partition's /dev/diskN NUMBER IS NOT STABLE

`panicpull.sh` hardcoded `/dev/disk4` for jobs 648-684. Job 687's probe found the
number differs between ramdisk sessions, and a wrong number returns **0 bytes
silently** rather than erroring - job 686 lost a result to exactly that.
**Fixed**: `panicpull.sh` now scans /dev/disk2..disk7, requires both a non-zero
read AND the `PEEP` record magic, prints what it tried, and says explicitly
"NO KERNEL PANIC WAS WRITTEN" when nothing matches. Old copy kept as
`panicpull.sh.pre-diskscan`.
Also recorded: job 687's probe used `grep -ac 'panic\|PEEP'`, which matched the
*word* "panic" in unrelated data on disk2/disk3 and looked like a hit. **Match on
the `PEEP` magic, not on the word.**

### R91.4 — FAULT 2: runtime logs are NOT on the volume we mount

/mnt1 is **disk1s1, the System volume**. Everything under its /var/logs,
/var/log and /var/mobile/Library/Logs is dated Jun 30 2020 - pristine from the
restore, because runtime writes go to the **Data volume (disk1s2)**. Every
"is there a log?" probe this project has run against /mnt1 was looking at the
wrong volume. The Data volume is an **unexplored observation channel** and is
exactly the "we need some observable" the app-session asked for in their §25.3;
CrashReporter reports there would name what died in a boot like Recipe L's,
without costing a panic.

### R91.5 — FAULT 3: two self-inflicted hangs, and the abort mechanism's real shape

  * An **unbounded `find` over a whole volume hangs the job** (job 690, ~4 min
    with no output). Then `mount_apfs -o ro /dev/disk1s2 /mnt4` itself wedged
    job 691 inside the pod-side ssh, where the abort file cannot reach it.
    **RULE: no unbounded find, and treat mounting the Data volume as risky until
    it is understood - depth-cap every search and bound every mount attempt.**
  * **`rm` is BLOCKED in the connected folder** ("Operation not permitted"), so
    I cannot clear `runner/abort` myself. The **runner clears it at the end of

    Mac). My earlier `rm -f abort` after job 677 appeared to work only because
    the runner had already done it. To withdraw a queued job, **`mv` it aside**

  * **The abort file only takes effect BETWEEN steps.** A `pod-sh` step already
    blocked inside a hung pod-side command keeps the runner busy regardless, so
    a wedged ramdisk needs the pod power-cycled to clear.

## R92 — RECIPE L RUN 2: the victim landed at chunk INDEX 1 and the write STAYED
## IN THE CHUNK (R88.4's bounded claim holds there) — but the neighbour was a
## FREE element, not our table. ONE GROOM OBJECT IS NOT ENOUGH.
## Plus a candidate in-image source for MANY groom objects.

Recipe L booted a second time, image byte-identical (R83 discipline). Baseline

unambiguously from this boot.

### R92.1 — The outcome VARIES between identical boots

    run 1 (16:57): NO kernel panic at all, ~30 s uptime, userspace restart
    run 2 (17:22): freed-element cookie panic, ~30-60 s uptime
**Same image, different outcome -> it is a lottery, not a deterministic loss.**
That answers the question R91.6 posed and it keeps retry on the table in
principle. It also means run 1's silence was NOT a win; it was a different loss.

### R92.2 — The decode, and the geometry closes perfectly this time

    panic(cpu 1 caller 0xfffffff01c6d3674): "a freed zone element has been
      modified in zone **kalloc.2048**: expected 0x5352156dd563f07 but found
      **0x650000f04a616371**, bits changed 0x603521a697375c76,
      **at offset 2040 of 2048** in element **0xfffffff00169a000**,
      cookies 0x3f0011b96541d032 0x5352156dd563f07"
    Kernel slide 0x0000000015000000; panicked task pid 0 kernel_task

`found` low 32 = our smalloc magic. high 32 = **0x650000f0** — note this is the
**word3/tag** field, not the size field: `0x65000000 | k` -> tag 0x65 = Recipe L,
**k = 0xf0 = 240**. So the matched qword is the one at tile offset k+8 = 248.
(Both halves of our 16-byte tile are now confirmed to read out usefully — R90.3's
dual-channel design working as intended.)

    dst = element + 2040 - 248 = 0xfffffff00169a700
    V   = dst + 256            = 0xfffffff00169a800
    element 0xfffffff00169a000 mod 4096 = 0      -> chunk **INDEX 0**
    V                          mod 4096 = 0x800  -> chunk **INDEX 1**
    write span [..a700, ..a800) lies wholly inside index 0

**Three things verified by this one panic:**
  1. **The victim landed at chunk index 1**, the favourable position - so the
     index-0 escape that produced R89 did NOT happen here.
  2. **The write stayed inside the 4 KiB chunk.** R88.4's bounded-write claim,
     which R89.3 had to qualify to "indices 1..7 only", is confirmed for index 1.
  3. `offset 2040 of 2048` is the **last 8 bytes** of the element - exactly where
     GROOM-ORDER said a free element keeps `old_head ^ cookie`, and
     `expected == cookies[1]` means `next == NULL`, i.e. it was the free list's
     last element. Their allocator model is now confirmed in fine detail.

### R92.3 — But we LOST, and the odds are worse than I said

The neighbour was a **free element**, not our merged table. Winning requires
BOTH:
    (a) the victim at chunk index 1  — happened here, and
    (b) our table being the index-0 element of THAT SAME chunk — did not.
I quoted 50% in R90.3 by only counting (a). With **one** groom object, plus three
boot jobs also allocating into kalloc.2048 (app-session §23.4), (b) is the hard
term and is unobservable — precisely their §25.3 point. **Correcting R90.3: one
groom object in an N=2 zone is a low-probability shot, not a coin flip.**
**=> In-image grooming with a single object is not a viable route. The high-N
approach (own ALL N of a chunk) is required, and that needs many same-size
persistent allocations we control.**

### R92.4 — A CANDIDATE IN-IMAGE SOURCE FOR MANY GROOM OBJECTS [hypothesis, for offline check]

We have been treating the merged table as our only in-image allocation. There
may be another, and it is attacker-sized and plural by construction:
**the `blkx` resources themselves.** The XML plist's `blkx` array holds N
separate base64 blobs; each is parsed into an OSData whose buffer is kalloc'd at
**the blob's own length, which we choose**, and a `mish` table of runCount r is
`0xcc + 40r` bytes — so r = 46 gives 2,044 B, landing in kalloc.2048.

If the resource dictionary stays retained for the duration of the attach, then
**N blkx resources = N live, same-size, attacker-chosen allocations**, which is
exactly the high-N groom set the plan needs, with no trust-cached binaries and no
planting. R75.3 records that the resources are released at attach step 5 (before
the read), which would kill it — **but that was about the fetched OSObject
references in the A1 array, not necessarily about the plist-owned OSData
buffers.** Worth separating those two lifetimes.

Note the coupling to watch: N resources contribute ~N*r runs to the merged table,
so with N=2 and r=46 the table is 0xf4+40*92 = 3,924 B (zone 4096) — it moves out
of kalloc.2048 as N grows, which is fine (we want it out of the victim's zone
anyway), but the arithmetic has to be done per N.

**This is an offline question** (does the plist/resource retention outlive the
merge, and is the OSData buffer exactly the blob length?) and therefore belongs
with the app-session rather than costing boots. Passing it to them.

Pod in DFU. Recipe L still armed in the snapshot. Panic region now holds run 2's
panic and **must be pulled or will be cleared by DumpPanic on any boot that
survives ~30 s** (R91.2). Nothing new armed; no boot is worth spending until
either the blkx-retention question (R92.4) or the app-session's trust-cached menu
gives us a high-N groom set.

## R93 *** kalloc.1664 IS VICTIM-REACHABLE AT dbr=3 — CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE. ***
## The one zone the whole plan depends on is validated, and the write landed
## EXACTLY ONE ELEMENT below the victim, mid-chunk, in a 17-element chunk.

Recipe M (job 695) booted ~17:36. the author: "stayed up for a bit after the setup
chime then pop crashed." Panic pulled by job 697.

### R93.1 — The result

    panic(cpu 0 caller 0xfffffff0204d3674): "a freed zone element has been
      modified in zone **kalloc.1664**: expected 0xfacadeb719a55633 but found
      **0x660000f04a616371**, bits changed 0x9ccade4753c43542,
      **at offset 1656 of 1664** in element **0xfffffff00136b000**,
      cookies 0x3f0011895cf3f1a2 0x5352147189252b3"
    Kernel slide 0x0000000018e00000; panicked task pid 55: xpcproxy

`found` low 32 = our smalloc magic; high 32 = **0x660000f0** = the word3/tag
field `0x66000000 | k` -> tag **0x66 = Recipe M**, **k = 240**. Fresh tag, so
this cannot be a stale Recipe L (0x65) or K (0x1800) log.

### R93.2 — THE FOUNDATIONAL CLAIM IS VALIDATED

The app-session's §26.1 narrowed the plan to a single zone on the argument that
`allocSize = buffersNeeded << 9` is always a multiple of 512, and that 1536 is
the only such value inside kalloc.1664's 1281..1664 window. **The panic names
`kalloc.1664`.** So `dbr = 3 -> allocSize 1536 -> kalloc.1664` is real, the
rounding model in kalloc_canblock behaves as modelled, and **the one zone the
entire aim plan now rests on is confirmed on hardware rather than on paper.**
(Also confirms the element size: "of 1664".)

### R93.3 — And the geometry is the cleanest we have had

    dst = element + 1656 - 248 = 0xfffffff00136b580
    V   = dst + 256            = 0xfffffff00136b680
    **V - element = 1664 exactly** -> the corrupted element is the IMMEDIATELY
      ADJACENT element below the victim
    alloc_size 28672 (7 pages, 17 elements):
      element mod 28672 = 0x2000 -> chunk **index 4**
      V       mod 28672 = 0x2680 -> chunk **index 5**
    offset 1656 of 1664 = the element's LAST 8 BYTES = the freelist cookie word

So: the victim landed **mid-chunk at index 5 of 17**, nowhere near index 0, the
write reached **exactly one element down**, and it stayed inside the chunk. Every
geometric property the plan needs is now demonstrated:
  * the zone is reachable (R93.2),
  * adjacency is element-granular and the reach lands on the neighbour's tail,
  * at N=17 the index-0 escape that produced R89 is a 1-in-17 edge case, and it
    did not occur.
We lost the 1-in-17 (the neighbour was a free element, not our merged table),
which is exactly the expected outcome with a single groom object.

### R93.4 — What is left, precisely

Everything except the groom set is now verified on hardware. The remaining gap is
the app-session's §27.2 condition: **K > F persistent same-size allocations in
kalloc.1664 (any size in 1281..1664), then free the last one, and the victim
lands on exactly that address in a chunk with no foreign elements.** Two open
sub-questions, both OFFLINE:
  1. **Where K comes from.** R92.4's blkx hypothesis fits this target well: a
     `mish` table of runCount r is `0xcc + 40r` bytes, so r = 27..36 gives
     1,284..1,644 B — squarely inside kalloc.1664's window. N blkx resources
     would then be N same-size allocations we author. Gated on whether the
     plist-owned OSData buffers outlive the merge.
  2. **Free-on-cue granularity.** If attach step 5 releases ALL resources, every
     groom object is freed at once and the victim's neighbours are free elements,
     which panic (R89/R92/R93 all show that detector firing). The §27.2 recipe
     needs the LAST one freed, not all of them. So the release granularity
     matters as much as the retention.

## R94 — POD-SIDE MEASUREMENTS THAT CLOSE TWO OF THE §30 NVRAM-ROUTE DEPENDENCIES,
## and the ONE question that now blocks the whole chain.

The app-session's §29 and §30 (their notes, 2,785 lines) between them answer both
questions R93.4 left open, and better than my blkx hypothesis:
  * **§29 — where K comes from**: six directories are ENUMERATED at boot and the
    reconstitute buffer is **per-vnode**, so **N copies of ONE in-window bundle at
    N paths yield N identical buffers**. 16 on-disk BUNDLE/DYLIB files land in
    1281..1664, and `/Library/Apple/Audio/Plug-Ins/HAL/` does not exist at
    baseline (zero baseline risk) with `mediaserverd` KeepAlive. Also a
    correction that killed my own framing: `dlopen` will not load an
    `MH_EXECUTE`, so all 75 candidates in their earlier count were unusable.
  * **§30 — a better source entirely**: the kernel's own NVRAM parser. An
    *invented* variable name falls off the 56-entry `gOFVariables` table and is
    parsed with the **terminator's own type = 4 (Data)**, producing an OSData
    whose buffer is `kalloc_canblock(&size,1,site)` with the size **UNROUNDED**
    — so 1281..1664 lands in kalloc.1664 exactly, and the primitive does not
    depend on page_shift at all. Created contiguously in one tight loop, persists
    the whole boot, and **the free is attacker-reachable** via
    `IONVRAM-DELETE-PROPERTY` in `setProperties` (root, no entitlement),
    freeing ONE chosen element.

### R94.1 — Measured on the pod: the NVRAM budget fits with ~3.7x margin [V]

Job 699, `nvram -p` in the ramdisk. **Names and lengths only; no values printed
anywhere — NVRAM holds the ECID, serials, MAC addresses and Wi-Fi secrets.**

    total dump bytes : 175
    variable count   : 10
    names: backlight-nits, bootdelay, SystemAudioVolumeSaved, backlight-level,
           debug-uarts, root-live-fs, nf-sync, nicsfix-pre, auto-boot, boot-args
    per-variable line lengths: 25, 11, 27, 23, 13, 14, 12, 16, 14, 10

The app-session parsed the author's NOR dumps and found `common` = **2048 bytes**. So
**~1,870 bytes are free**. At their 0xFF-escape figure (~31 bytes of partition
per 1,664-byte OSData), **16 groom variables cost ~500 bytes — it fits about
3.7x over.** The budget is not a constraint.

### R94.2 — Measured on the pod: ramdisk-written NVRAM DOES reach the next boot's
### `nvram-proxy-data` [V, and it was already in our own data]

`root-live-fs`, `nf-sync` and `nicsfix-pre` are all present in the live dump and
**all three were written from ramdisk jobs** (`nvram -s root-live-fs=1` runs at
the end of every imgswap script; nf-sync/nicsfix-pre are from the R59-R61
persistence work). So the groom variables can be planted from an ordinary ramdisk
job and iBoot will hand them to the kernel as proxy data on the next cold boot.
**No need to write NVRAM from the booted system.** `nvram` is at
`/usr/sbin/nvram` in the ramdisk and on the system volume (54,256 B, R64).

### R94.3 — THE ONE QUESTION THAT NOW BLOCKS THE CHAIN

§27.2's deterministic recipe needs the free to happen **after** the K allocations
and **before** the victim's allocation. §30 supplies a free that is reachable in
principle — but **nothing identified so far CALLS it at the right moment**:
  * `IONVRAM-DELETE-PROPERTY` goes through `setProperties`, i.e. it needs a
    userspace process to issue `IORegistryEntrySetCFProperties`.
  * We cannot supply argv: §13 closed the MRM cache (no signature to forge,
    cdhash content-derived), and §8 established that the 11 RunAtLoad root jobs
    pass **no non-dash arguments** — so `nvram -d <ourvar>` is not reachable by
    host substitution.

**Proposed way around it, and the question to put to the app-session:**
> **Does any boot-time Apple process DELETE or CLEAR an NVRAM variable, which
> one, and does it happen before `UserEventAgent` starts?** If so, give our groom
> object that variable's name and **Apple's own code performs the free on cue**,
> with no argv and no new host.
There is already circumstantial support in our own notes: R63 found
`CleanupPreparePathService` reverting state on every boot, and R59-R61
established that `root-live-fs` is read every boot. A one-shot boot flag that is
cleared after being read is exactly the shape needed.
Sub-questions: (a) is `IODTNVRAM::removeProperty` (0xfffffff007bd4cf0) reached
from anything other than `setProperties`? (b) is the free needed at all, or can K
be chosen so the intermediate chunk holds exactly 16 of 17 ours — which needs F,
the pre-existing free count in kalloc.1664, and is probably unknowable?

Also flagging their own §29.2 note: **`UserEventAgent` is both our hdik host for
steps 1-3 and one of the enumerated-directory grooming hosts.** Using it for both
at once needs resolving before any recipe is built on it.

## R95 — THEIR §34 KILLED MY BLKX IDEA (correctly) AND REPLACED IT WITH A BETTER
## SELF-GROOMING RECIPE. One inconsistency found in it, and RECIPE N tests the one
## claim underneath it that is undecidable offline.

### R95.1 — My R92.4 blkx hypothesis is DEAD, and the kill is sound

Their §34 (PATH-AUDIT) closed it two ways, and the first was one instruction past
where I stopped looking:
  * the instruction after the resource release loop is `blr [vt+0x5d8]` ->
    `0xfffffff007dcd6d0`, the plist teardown, which releases the whole
    OSDictionary/OSArray/OSData graph — **freeing in-window container backing
    arrays** (OSDictionary = 16*capacity, in-window at capacity 81..104).
    kalloc.1664 is zone index 20, outside the 0x27fff caching bitmap, so plain
    LIFO — **those frees land in front of ours.**
  * blkx parse and `read()` are different top-level kernel entries with nub
    publication, IOBlockStorageDriver matching, IOMedia publication and the
    APM/GPT probe in between — **358 unresolved virtual call sites**. Not
    statically closable.
Recording this because R92.4 was mine and it was wrong for a reason I could have
found: I reasoned about the release loop without reading past its end.

### R95.2 — The replacement is better: THE READ LOOP GROOMS ITSELF

  * The victim is `IOMalloc`'d and `IOFree`'d **inside every loop iteration**, so
    the element sits at the free-list head for the next iteration. **That is the
    timed free, for free** — no NVRAM, no `keybagd`, no persistent NOR write.
  * `KDIUDIFCacheBuffer::setLength` does `IOMalloc(runSectorCount * 512)` and
    short-circuits when capacity already suffices. So with every zlib run at the
    SAME sector count = 3 (`allocSize` 1536 -> kalloc.1664), **the cache takes
    its depth buffers once at exactly the victim's size and goes quiet** —
    persistent, late-placed, in-window neighbours acquired right beside the
    victim, from our own image's run geometry.
  * Trap they flagged: **a cache HIT skips the victim IOMalloc**, so every zlib
    run needs a DISTINCT sector range.
  * They also corrected themselves usefully: `R != sum(r_i)` (four `w25`
    increments: leading gaps, kept/clipped runs, tail gap, terminator), the
    kernel REPAIRS geometry itself (inserts gaps, skips, clips — coverage need
    not be contiguous), zero-length runs are accepted and counted, and the
    OSData byte length is independent of `blocksRunCount` because the merge only
    calls `getBytesNoCopy`, never `getLength`. So `r` is far more freely
    authorable than either of us assumed.

### R95.3 — INCONSISTENCY IN THEIR §34.9, and it is the top question for them

§34.9 carries forward **16/17 = 94.1%** from §27.3. But §27.3's figure is
`(N-1)/N` for **owning N-1 of N elements**. The new groom set is **the cache's
buffers, and `cache-depth` defaults to 5** (§34.6). Owning 5 of 17 gives
P(neighbour is ours) ~= **5/16 ~= 31%**, not 94%. The aim figure does not follow
from the new groom set.

**So `cache-depth` is not a side question about suppression — it IS the groom-set
size, and therefore IS the aim probability.** Their §34.10 lists it as "whether
cache-depth can be set to 0 ... and where that property comes from"; it should be
the top item, reframed:
> **Where does `getProperty("cache-depth")` read from, and can WE set it from the
> image's resource-fork plist or the attach request? If it can be set to 16, aim
> goes from ~31% to 94.1%.**
This is also a resurfacing of OUR OWN R78.4 open question, which already found
`nEntries = getProperty("cache-depth")` with no constant anywhere and noted "if
cache-depth is settable in the attach request's property dictionary (which for
DiskImages originates in userspace), the spray width is attacker-chosen."

A second, independent ceiling worth their attention: with `allocSize` 1536 the
runs are 3 sectors each, and only sectors 0-15 are read, so **one probe read can
hold at most 5 zlib runs** — which happens to equal the default depth. More
groom buffers therefore need MORE READS, and R87 already proved READ #2 fires at
an offset AND LENGTH we choose (`PartitionEntryLBA`, `NumberOfEntries x
SizeOfEntry`). 64 entries x 128 = 8,192 B at a chosen LBA = 16 more sectors = 5
more runs. **So the scaling path for the groom set is GPT READ #2, not a bigger
cache** — and that half is already hardware-verified.

### R95.4 — RECIPE N (job 700, armed, CHECKPOINT PASSED, 3,334 B)

Their §34.10 lists the attach->probe gap as honestly undecidable offline. Fine —
but there is a different claim underneath §34.9 that is ALSO hardware-only and
has never been exercised: **does `read()` actually iterate over more than one
zlib run inside the single 8,192-byte probe read?** R75.3 established read() is a
loop (`cbnz x22` @0xdcb5f4, one iteration per chunk), but **every recipe this
project has booted had exactly ONE chunk in sectors 0-15, so the loop has never
run twice.** R85's "one write per boot" measured one read REQUEST, not one
ITERATION — and the whole self-grooming recipe depends on the difference.

    run A  sectors 0-2  zlib, compOff 0, compLen 21 — a REAL zlib stream of
           1,536 bytes, so it DECOMPRESSES SUCCESSFULLY: full victim
           IOMalloc/IOFree, populates the cache, and does NOT underflow
    run B  sectors 3-5  zlib, compOff 0x15, compLen 1,792 = allocSize + 256
           -> THE UNDERFLOW WRITE, payload tag **0x67**, size base 0x2400
    distinct sector ranges so the cache cannot short-circuit run B
    dbr = 3 -> allocSize 1536 -> kalloc.1664 (R93-confirmed)
    runCount 4 -> merged table 404 B -> kalloc.512, far outside the window

    tag 0x67 present  -> read() DOES loop; the self-grooming foundation holds,
                         the cache groom set is reachable, and R85 must be
                         re-scoped from "one write" to "one request".
    nothing           -> the loop stopped after run A. Their recipe needs
                         rethinking BEFORE it is built, which is the whole point
                         of testing it now.

### R95.5 — Division of labour from here

**Them (offline):** (1) where `cache-depth` comes from and whether we can set it
— it is the aim probability (R95.3); (2) census the NON-constant-size allocation
sites reachable from the probe path, since their §34.8 bound covers only the 33
constant-size ones; (3) their held §34.9 image.
**Us (pod):** (1) Recipe N — does the loop iterate; (2) if yes, Recipe O =
GPT bait with READ #2 sized to 8,192 B at a chosen LBA, giving 5 runs in
sectors 0-15 plus 5 more at the chosen LBA -> ~10 cache buffers, poisoned run
last. That scales the groom set with hardware we have already proved, without
waiting on the cache-depth answer.

## R96 — RECIPE N: FULLY CLEAN BOOT, ALL THE WAY TO SLEEP. The healthiest the pod
## has ever been with a write armed — but the result is AMBIGUOUS, and R96.2 says
## why. RECIPE N2 armed to disambiguate with one changed variable.

### R96.1 — The observation

Recipe N (job 700) booted ~18:42. the author: "booted up normally for a few minutes with
no crash", then "still no crash, let it run long enough that it went to sleep."
**The pod reached an idle/sleep state.** Every prior recipe with a poisoned chunk
crashed within 6-60 s; Recipe G (the only other clean run) had NO poisoned chunk
in the read range at all. So this is the first clean-to-sleep boot with an
underflow-capable image armed.

### R96.2 — Why this is NOT yet a win, stated plainly

A quiet boot is consistent with two very different worlds and delta = 256 cannot
separate them:

  (i)  **read() never reached run B.** Only run A (a valid zlib stream) was
       processed, no underflow write happened, and the clean boot means nothing.
       The loop at 0xfffffff007dcb5f4 would then not iterate across chunks within
       one request, and the app-session's §34.9 self-grooming recipe collapses.
  (ii) **read() DID reach run B, and the write landed on run A's own cache
       buffer.** `KDIUDIFCacheBuffer::setLength` IOMallocs
       `runSectorCount * 512` = 1,536 B -> kalloc.1664 — **exactly the victim's
       size and zone**. Run A's buffer is therefore a live, in-window neighbour
       sitting right where the next victim allocates. Overwriting it is harmless
       because nothing re-reads sectors 0-2. **That is precisely the mechanism
       §34.9 is designed to produce, i.e. the best result of the project.**

Both predict silence. **I am not calling this a win on the strength of a quiet
boot**, and nobody downstream should build on it until N2 settles it.

### R96.3 — RECIPE N2 (job 701, armed, CHECKPOINT PASSED, 7,174 B)

Changes **exactly one variable** from N:

    delta 256 -> **4096**   (L = 1536 + 4096 = 5632)

Justification for 4,096 as the discriminator: a 4,096-byte reach was fatal in
**R79, R80, R81 and R82 — four for four, across three different zones**
(kalloc.512 pmap-adjacent, ipc_entry, Sandbox smalloc, strncmp key pointer). It
is the best-evidenced "if this write happens, the machine dies" setting we have.

Everything else byte-identical to N: same run A zlib stream (verified to
decompress to 1,536 B), same sector ranges 0-2 and 3-5, same dbr = 3 ->
allocSize 1536 -> kalloc.1664. Fresh tag **0x68** and size base **0x2800** so N
and N2 results can never be confused, and so a stale log cannot masquerade.

    CRASH -> read() DOES loop across chunks within one request. World (i) is
             dead, §34.9's foundation holds, and **R85 must be re-scoped from
             "one write per boot" to "one read REQUEST per boot"** — a materially
             different claim that changes the grooming ceiling.
    QUIET -> the loop genuinely stops after run A. World (ii) is dead. The
             self-grooming recipe then has to be rebuilt around more READS (the
             GPT READ #2 path, hardware-proved in R87, where we choose both
             PartitionEntryLBA and NumberOfEntries x SizeOfEntry) rather than
             more runs per read.

Deliberately spending this boot BEFORE the app-session finishes building its
§34.9 image, since a negative would invalidate the design rather than the build.


================================================================================
R97. RECIPE N2 WAS SILENT, AND THE REASON REWRITES THE GROOM PROBLEM.
     The probe reads 512 bytes, read() loops on remaining sectors, and the
     victim is allocated AND FREED on every pass.
================================================================================

Job 701 armed Recipe N2 (7,174 B, CHECKPOINT PASSED). the author cold-booted it and it
did not crash. A reach of 4096 B had been fatal in R79, R80, R81 and R82 - four
for four, across three different zones - so the honest first reading was that
the underflow write had not happened at all.

That turned out to be exactly right, for a reason that had nothing to do with
the write primitive.

R97.1  FIRST, EXCLUDE THE CHEAP EXPLANATION.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If run A's zlib stream had been malformed, read() would have errored at chunk 0
and never advanced to run B - which would look identical to "the loop does not
iterate", and would have sent us down the wrong road. So I parsed the shipped
images back off disk (koly trailer -> XML plist -> mish table -> runs) and
inflated run A with the same parameters the kernel uses:

    recipeN2.dmg  (7,174 B)   dbr 3 -> allocSize 1536
      run0 ZLIB   sec 0+3    compOff 0     compLen 21      -> inflates to 1536 B  MATCH
      run1 ZLIB   sec 3+3    compOff 21    compLen 5632     poisoned, delta 4096
      run2 IGNORE sec 6+8186
      run3 TERM   sec 8192
    recipeN1664.dmg (3,334 B) identical but run1 compLen 1792 (delta 256)

Run A is a VALID stream inflating to exactly 1536 bytes in both images, and the
geometry is coherent. The "run A errored and bailed" explanation is dead. The
images were built correctly; the experiment was aimed wrong.

R97.2  *** THE PARTITION PROBE READS 512 BYTES, NOT 8 KB. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Both this log and the app-session's notes (their SS9, SS34.9, and the line
"0-15 are read, so one probe read holds at most 5 zlib runs") assumed the probe
reads the first 8 KB. It does not. From IOGUIDPartitionScheme's probe
(VAs; file = VA - 0xfffffff007004000, __TEXT_EXEC, filesize == vmsize):

    0xfffffff007cd6574  blr  [x22 vt +0x5a0]      -> x23 = blockSize
    0xfffffff007cd658c  and  x8, x23, #0x1ff       blockSize must be a 512 multiple
    0xfffffff007cd6594  ccmp w0, #0, #4, eq
    0xfffffff007cd6598  b.eq -> bail
    0xfffffff007cd659c  add  x8, x23, #0x1ff       roundup(512, blockSize)
    0xfffffff007cd65a0  udiv x8, x8, x23             == 1 for any blockSize >= 512
    0xfffffff007cd65a4  mul  x0, x8, x23             == blockSize   <<< THE LENGTH
    0xfffffff007cd65b0  bl   0xfffffff007bbc764     allocate that buffer -> x21
    0xfffffff007cd65fc  mov  x2, #0                 MBR     read @ byte 0,   512 B
    0xfffffff007cd660c  blr  [x22 vt +0x548]
    0xfffffff007cd6624  ldrh w8,[x0,#0x1fe]         0xAA55 at byte 510
    0xfffffff007cd6690  mov  x2, x23                GPT hdr read @ byte 512, 512 B

TWO 512-BYTE READS, at sector 0 and sector 1. Nothing else on the disk is read
unless a header we control says where to look. One fact, and it retro-explains
the entire series:

  - B/D/E/F put the poisoned chunk at sector 0. Fired every time. Sector 0 is
    the first thing read.
  - G (R85): benign sectors 0-15, poison at 16-112. NOTHING fired. I recorded
    that as "the reader touches only sectors 0-15". Wrong reason, right data:
    nothing ever read sector 16.
  - J (R87): fired at sector 64 only because PartitionEntryLBA sent READ #2
    there. That was never evidence of a wide read; it was evidence of a
    DIRECTED one.
  - N and N2: run A sectors 0-2, run B sectors 3-5. A 512-byte read at sector 0
    is satisfied inside run A. RUN B WAS NEVER REQUESTED.

So R85's conclusion "one write per boot, at sector 0 only" was an artefact of
our bait, not a property of the kernel - and R96.2's interpretation (ii), that
Recipe N's clean boot showed self-grooming working, is withdrawn. Nothing was
grooming. Nothing past run A ran.

R97.3  READ #2's LENGTH AND OFFSET ARE BOTH OURS, AND ITS CRC IS CHECKED LATE.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    0xfffffff007cd66d0  ldr  w2,[x24,#0xc]      HeaderSize
    0xfffffff007cd66d4  cmp  w2,#0x5c           >= 92 ...
    0xfffffff007cd66d8  ccmp x23, x2, #0, hs    ... and <= blockSize
    0xfffffff007cd66e4  str  wzr,[x24,#0x10]    zero the CRC field
    0xfffffff007cd66f0  bl   0xfffffff0077a2c14 crc32(header, HeaderSize)
    0xfffffff007cd66f4  cmp  w0,w25 / b.ne      *** the HEADER CRC gates us ***
    0xfffffff007cd66fc  ldr  w25,[x24,#0x54]    SizeOfEntry
    0xfffffff007cd6700  sub  w8,w25,#0x80
    0xfffffff007cd6704  lsr  w8,w8,#7
    0xfffffff007cd6708  cmp  w8,#0x1fe / b.hi   => 128 <= eSz
    0xfffffff007cd6710  ldr  w26,[x24,#0x50]    NumberOfEntries
    0xfffffff007cd6714  lsr  w8,w26,#0x10
    0xfffffff007cd6718  cbnz w8 -> bail         => nEnt <= 0xFFFF
    0xfffffff007cd6720  ldr  x28,[x24,#0x48]    PartitionEntryLBA
    0xfffffff007cd679c  mul  w24,w26,w25        nEnt * eSz
    0xfffffff007cd67a0  add  x8, x23, x24       roundup to blockSize
    0xfffffff007cd67ac  mul  x0, x8, x23        <<< READ #2's LENGTH
    0xfffffff007cd67bc  bl   0xfffffff007bbc764 allocate it
    0xfffffff007cd67c8  mul  x2, x28, x23       byteStart = PLBA * blockSize
    0xfffffff007cd67e8  blr  [x22 vt +0x548]    READ #2
    0xfffffff007cd680c  bl   crc32 / cmp w0,w27 the ARRAY crc, AFTER the read

The entry-array CRC32 is verified AFTER READ #2 returns, so our write has
already landed by the time it is computed. We never have to make it match. Only
the header CRC gates us, and that is zlib.crc32 bit-for-bit (table at
0xfffffff00700bd58, reflected poly 0xEDB88320, confirmed in R87).

Bytes 0x38-0x47 (DiskGUID) are byte-swapped at 0xcd6724-0xcd6760 and formatted
into a property via 0xfffffff007b60f5c; never validated. Free field.

R97.4  *** read() LOOPS OVER RUNS, GATED ON REMAINING SECTORS. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    0xfffffff007dcb434  (loop body top: fetch run, decode type)
    ...
    0xfffffff007dcb5a4  ldur x9,[x29,#-0x60]    sectors consumed this pass
    0xfffffff007dcb5a8  sub  x22, x22, x9       x22 = REMAINING sectors
    0xfffffff007dcb5ac  add  x28, x9, x28
    0xfffffff007dcb5b0  add  x23, x9, x23
    0xfffffff007dcb5b4  add  x21, x21, x9, lsl #9   output pointer advances
    0xfffffff007dcb5d4  cmp  w8, #0x3b          state dispatch
    0xfffffff007dcb5e8  movk w10, #2, lsl #16   mask 0x00020001
    0xfffffff007dcb5f4  cbnz x22, 0xfffffff007dcb434   <<< LOOP WHILE SECTORS REMAIN
    0xfffffff007dcb5f8  b    0xfffffff007dcb91c        <<< else done

"Serve what you can, advance, repeat." N2 is now fully explained: a 1-sector
request consumed 1 sector out of run A, x22 went to 0, the loop exited. Run B
was never reached. The write primitive was never in question.

METHOD NOTE, and the third instance of one bug class. My automated back-edge
scan missed 0xdcb5f4 entirely, because it tested `op_str.startswith('#')` and
`cbnz x22, #0x...` begins with `x22`. R72 was `int('#0x..',0)` raising on
capstone's '#' prefix; R-series was the bare `except` that swallowed it; this is
the same family again - a parser that silently declines the operand form that
matters. The loop was found by READING the dispatch block, not by the scan.
Rule: a control-flow scan that reports no back-edges in a function that
obviously has them is reporting a decoder bug, not a finding.

R97.5  *** THE VICTIM IS allocSize, AND IT IS FREED ON EVERY PASS. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    0xfffffff007dcb5fc  lsl  x20, x9, #9        x20 = uncompressed length
    0xfffffff007dcb600  cmp  w10, #5            entryType == zlib
    0xfffffff007dcb60c  ldr  x8,[x24,#0xb0]
    0xfffffff007dcb610  ldr  w8,[x8,#0x20]      decompressBufferRequested
    0xfffffff007dcb614  lsl  w8, w8, #9         allocSize = dbr << 9
    0xfffffff007dcb618  cmp  x20, x8
    0xfffffff007dcb61c  b.ls 0xfffffff007dcb658 uncompressed <= allocSize (<=, so
                                                 the equality edge passes - which
                                                 M/N/R93 already proved in silicon)
    0xfffffff007dcb658  mov  x19, x8
    0xfffffff007dcb660  bl   0xfffffff007b7bdf0 IOMalloc(allocSize)  -> x20
    0xfffffff007dcb674  bl   0xfffffff007c40700
    0xfffffff007dcb678  str  x19,[sp,#0x28]     keep allocSize for the free
    0xfffffff007dcb67c  add  x8, x20, x19       bufEnd = buf + allocSize
    0xfffffff007dcb680  ldp  x2, x1,[sp,#0x58]  x2 = compressedLength
    0xfffffff007dcb684  sub  x19, x8, x2        dst = bufEnd - compressedLength
    0xfffffff007dcb6a0  blr  [vt +0x590]        *** THE WRITE ***
    0xfffffff007dcb6bc  bl   0xfffffff007dcdd08 inflate
    0xfffffff007dcb6d8  bl   0xfffffff007c40550 memcpy out, consumed << 9
    0xfffffff007dcb6e4  bl   0xfffffff007dccbe0 } cache insert path
    0xfffffff007dcb6f4  bl   0xfffffff007dcc904 }
    0xfffffff007dcb708  bl   0xfffffff007dccbf0 }
    0xfffffff007dcb710  mov  x0, x20
    0xfffffff007dcb714  ldr  x1,[sp,#0x28]
    0xfffffff007dcb718  bl   0xfffffff007b7be48 *** IOFree(victim, allocSize) ***
    0xfffffff007dcb730  b    0xfffffff007dcb5a4 loop

Two corrections to this log fall out of that block:

 (a) The victim is IOMalloc(allocSize) with allocSize = dbr << 9. It is NOT
     runSectorCount * 512. The note in the summary that
     "KDIUDIFCacheBuffer::setLength -> IOMalloc(runSectorCount * 512)" describes
     a DIFFERENT allocation (the cache buffer, inserted at 0xdccbe0/0xdcc904);
     the buffer that receives our write is this one. For every recipe so far the
     two coincided because sectorCount * 512 == allocSize by construction, so no
     earlier finding changes - but the victim ZONE is selected by dbr ALONE,
     independent of run geometry. That is a freer parameter than we thought.

 (b) bufEnd = buf + allocSize, so describe()'s dst arithmetic was right and my
     first reaction to it was wrong. Noted against myself.

R97.6  *** WHAT THIS MEANS: WE WERE SOLVING THE WRONG PROBLEM. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Alloc -> write -> inflate -> copy out -> FREE -> loop. The zone free list is
per-chunk LIFO (R-series), so iteration N+1's IOMalloc(allocSize) pops back the
element iteration N just freed. In a multi-run read, EVERY RUN WRITES FROM THE
SAME VICTIM ADDRESS V.

Step 4 has spent R88-R96 hunting a persistent same-size groom set in order to
win a 1-in-17 adjacency lottery once per boot. That is the wrong problem. What
the loop actually offers:

  - land V ONCE, and then take as many writes as we care to put runs in the
    read - each with its own compressedLength (hence its own reach) and its own
    content, all from the same base, all in ONE boot;
  - the number of runs is bounded by nEnt * eSz (R97.3), i.e. by us, not by
    cache-depth 5 (which the app-session established in their SS36 is not
    settable);
  - and because the reach is per-run, a single read can SWEEP: run k writes at
    V - 512k with a tag naming k. One boot maps what lives below V.

So the aim problem reduces from "get N persistent same-size allocations and win
adjacency" to "characterise what sits below one V, then write to it". And the
sweep is self-reporting: whichever k detonates tells us the offset.

The app-session's SS34.9 mechanism (the read loop grooms itself) survives in
spirit and dies in detail: the loop does provide the repetition, but not as a
groom SET - it provides repetition at a FIXED ADDRESS, which is strictly better
and needs no groom set at all. Their SS27.2 "K > F allocations, free the last,
victim lands there deterministically" is the same insight; the loop hands it to
us for free, with no external allocation source needed.

R97.7  RECIPE O - the controlled experiment, built and self-verified.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
recipeO1664.dmg, 20,188 B, built by mkrecipeO.py. Minimal delta from Recipe J,
which is the only image proven to pass the GPT gates and fire READ #2 (R87).

    sectors 0-15    RAW     protective MBR + GPT header. No allocation, no write.
    sectors 16-63   ignore
    sectors 64-66   ZLIB    BENIGN. Real stream, compLen 40, inflates to exactly
                            1536. dst = bufEnd - 40, stays inside its own
                            element. Its only job is to be run #1.
    sectors 67-69   ZLIB    POISONED tag 0x69, L 5632, dst = V - 4096. LAST on
                            purpose.
    sectors 70-8190 ignore
    sector 8191     ZLIB    POISONED tag 0x6A, L 4608, dst = V - 3072. The
                            ALTERNATE header LBA - a path discriminator.
    terminator 8192
    dbr 3 -> allocSize 1536 -> kalloc.1664 (R93-proven reachable, element-granular)
    header CRC32 0x0f694c69, PLBA 64, nEnt 24 x eSz 128 = 3072 B = 6 sectors
    => READ #2 spans sectors 64..69, i.e. BOTH runs.

CONTROL. dbr, allocSize, zone, run geometry, L and reach are all IDENTICAL to
Recipe N2's run B, which was silent. The single difference is that the read
request now spans both runs. Nothing else varies.

FALSIFIABLE PREDICTIONS. The poisoned run is last so that silence is as
informative as a panic:

  tag 0x69  -> one read request iterates across runs, as R97.4 derives. The
               fixed-address multi-write of R97.6 is available, and Recipe P can
               be the sweep.
  tag 0x6A  -> the primary header was rejected and the alternate was read. Still
               a second read, but fix the header before believing anything else.
  NO PANIC  -> read() serves at most ONE run per request regardless of how much
               is asked for, which would CONTRADICT R97.4's decode and mean I
               have misread the latch. Then multi-run writing is dead, N2 is
               explained by something else, and the groom sources left are
               repeated probe reads or the app-session's SS29 (directories) /
               SS30 (NVRAM).
  tag 0x5A-0x68 -> stale log from Recipes D-N2, not this experiment.

Because R97.4 is a decode rather than a measurement, three claims in it are
being re-derived independently from the binary by a separate agent that has not
seen my working: the loop condition, the allocSize victim, and the
per-iteration free. Agent output is model output and carries no authority; it is
a second decode to disagree with mine, nothing more.

R97.8  THE ZONE TABLE, AUTHORITATIVE - AND R97.6's LIFO ASSUMPTION CONFIRMED.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R97.6 only works if kalloc.1664 is NOT a per-CPU caching zone: a caching zone
routes frees through a magazine and the next allocation does not necessarily pop
back what was just freed. So I read k_zone_cfg (VA 0xfffffff0074a4810,
__DATA_CONST, filesize == vmsize) directly rather than reasoning from the
bitmap alone.

Struct is 16 bytes: {u32 caching_flag; u32 elem_size; packed_ptr name}. The name
pointers are CHAINED-FIXUP PACKED - only the low 48 bits are the VA and the high
16 are a fixup tag, so a naive 8-byte read yields 0x0027fff0........ and looks
like garbage. Mask to 48 bits and restore the canonical top bits.

  idx  flag  elem   name            caching (bitmap 0x27fff)
   0    1      16   kalloc.16       CACHING
   1    1      32   kalloc.32       CACHING
   2    1      48   kalloc.48       CACHING
   3    1      64   kalloc.64       CACHING
   4    1      80   kalloc.80       CACHING
   5    1      96   kalloc.96       CACHING
   6    1     128   kalloc.128      CACHING
   7    1     160   kalloc.160      CACHING
   8    1     192   kalloc.192      CACHING
   9    1     224   kalloc.224      CACHING
  10    1     256   kalloc.256      CACHING
  11    1     288   kalloc.288      CACHING
  12    1     368   kalloc.368      CACHING
  13    1     400   kalloc.400      CACHING
  14    1     512   kalloc.512      CACHING
  15    0     576   kalloc.576      -
  16    0     768   kalloc.768      -
  17    1    1024   kalloc.1024     CACHING
  18    0    1152   kalloc.1152     -
  19    0    1280   kalloc.1280     -
  20    0    1664   kalloc.1664     -
  21    0    2048   kalloc.2048     -
  22    0    4096   kalloc.4096     -
  23    0    6144   kalloc.6144     -
  24    0    8192   kalloc.8192     -
  25    0   16384   kalloc.16384    -
  26    0   32768   kalloc.32768    -

The per-entry flag field and the 0x27fff bitmap agree bit for bit on all 27
entries - two independent encodings of the same fact, which is the verification
I wanted rather than one source twice.

 (a) *** kalloc.1664 (index 20) IS NOT A CACHING ZONE. *** No magazine. Frees go
     straight to the per-chunk LIFO free list, so pass N+1's IOMalloc(1536) pops
     back exactly the element pass N freed. R97.6's fixed-address multi-write
     stands for the zone Recipe O actually uses. Same for 768, 1152, 1280, 2048,
     4096, 6144, 8192 - every zone we have ever panicked in except 512.

 (b) RETRACTION OF TWO "CORRECTIONS" I ALMOST FILED HERE. On first writing this
     section I logged kalloc.512-is-caching and kalloc.12288-does-not-exist as
     new findings. Neither is. JOB-PREFLIGHT.md already carries both, verbatim,
     at the R75 rules: the caching == 1 / caching == 0 lists are there in full
     and correct, 512 is named in them, and the line "1536, 2560 and 3072 DO NOT
     EXIST on 17M61 ... Largest zone is 32768" already states the ladder. The
     12288 was a slip in MY recall during this session, not an error in the
     project's notes, and the preflight needed no fix.
     Logging that distinction rather than quietly deleting it, because a false
     correction in this file is more expensive than a missing one: a future pass
     would trust it and re-derive against a phantom error. The rule the preflight
     already states stands unchanged - never groom in a caching zone, and dbr 1
     (allocSize 512) is unreproducible by construction.

  (c) 576 and 1152 are non-caching and sit either side of 768, which is where the
     R89 panic landed. If Recipe O confirms iteration, a dbr of 2 (1024, CACHING
     - avoid), 3 (1536 -> 1664), or 5 (2560 -> no such zone, rounds to 4096) are
     the practical choices. dbr 3 remains the right one.

R97.9  INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION OF R97.4/.5/.6 - ALL THREE CONFIRMED, WITH
       FOUR CORRECTIONS, AND THE CLAMP MAKES RECIPE O's CASE STRONGER.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A separate agent re-derived the three load-bearing claims from the binary with
its own decoder, having not seen my working. It hand-verified its decoder by
re-encoding six instructions from the ARM ARM against the raw LE words, and it
took function bounds from LC_FUNCTION_STARTS (file off 0x17b4000, 65,139
entries) rather than guessing: the containing function is
[0xfffffff007dcb3bc .. 0xfffffff007dcb96c), and both 0xdcb434 (+0x78) and
0xdcb5a4 (+0x1e8) are interior to it. LC_SYMTAB has nsyms = 0 - the cache is
stripped - so every NAME in R97 is inferred from structure and dataflow, never
read from a symbol. Worth stating plainly in this log.

Agent output is model output and carries no authority. What makes this useful is
not that it agreed but that it disagreed in four specific, checkable places.

 (a) *** CORRECTION: THE CONSUMED COUNT IS CLAMPED. *** I implied nothing bounds
     it. Wrong:
        0xfffffff007dcb4e0  ldp  x9, x8, [sp,#0x68]   x9=runSectors x8=runStart
        0xfffffff007dcb4e4  sub  x27, x23, x8         offset into the run
        0xfffffff007dcb4e8  sub  x8, x9, x27          sectors available from here
        0xfffffff007dcb4ec  cmp  x8, x22
        0xfffffff007dcb4f0  csel x11, x22, x8, gt     x11 = min(avail, remaining)
        0xfffffff007dcb4f4  stur x11, [x29,#-0x60]    the slot the latch reloads
     The other writer of that slot, callee 0xfffffff007dcc6fc (reached by bl at
     0xdcb464 with x3 = x29-0x60), clamps identically: 0xdcc748 cmp x10,x2 /
     0xdcc74c csel x13,x2,x10,gt / 0xdcc76c str x13,[x3], with x2 = x22 from
     0xdcb460. So `sub x22,x22,x9` cannot underflow.
     THIS STRENGTHENS RECIPE O RATHER THAN THREATENING IT. Walk it:
       request 6 sectors at 64; run 1 = sectors 64..66
       x27 = 64-64 = 0 ; avail = 3-0 = 3 ; 3 > 6 false -> x11 = 3
       latch: x22 = 6-3 = 3 ; x23 = 67 ; x21 += 3*512
       cbnz x22 (=3) -> loop -> the run at sector 67, which is the poisoned one.
     min(available, remaining) is exactly the "serve what you can, advance,
     repeat" model R97.4 asserted. The clamp is the mechanism, not a limit on it.

 (b) CORRECTION: 0xdcb5a4 has SIX predecessors and TWO back-edges, not one -
     0xdcb730 (-396, our path) and 0xdcb910 (-876). 0xdcb434 has exactly one
     back-edge (0xdcb5f4) plus fallthrough from the preheader 0xdcb430.
     0xdcb910 is the continue of a SECOND allocation path, reached after its own
     frees at 0xdcb8ec/0xdcb8f8. That path (entered at 0xdcb630, the
     non-entryType-5 branch) makes TWO allocations - 0xdcb73c and 0xdcb754, both
     bl 0xfffffff007b7bdf0. Noted for later: more allocations per run means more
     free-list churn per iteration, which matters if we ever mix run types.

 (c) *** CORRECTION: THE LATCH IS STATUS-GATED BEFORE THE cbnz. ***
        0xfffffff007dcb5d4  cmp  w8, #0x3b
        0xfffffff007dcb5d8  b.hi 0xfffffff007dcb960
        0xfffffff007dcb5ec  tst  x9, x10          x10 = 0x20001
        0xfffffff007dcb5f0  b.eq 0xfffffff007dcb948
     The loop continues only when the status code's bit lands in mask 0x20001,
     i.e. code 0 or 17. So the rule is "while sectors remain AND status is OK",
     and 0xdcb91c is one of three exits, not the only one.
     THIS RETROSPECTIVELY JUSTIFIES R97.1. Had run A's zlib stream been
     malformed, the status gate - not the sector count - would have ended the
     loop before run B. Validating run A offline was not belt-and-braces; it was
     the difference between a controlled experiment and an uninterpretable one.
     Recipe O's run 1 is a real stream that inflates to exactly 1536 B, so it
     returns status 0 and the gate passes.

 (d) PRECISION on R97.5: x20 at 0xdcb618 is the FULL RUN's uncompressed length
     (x9 << 9, from [sp,#0x68], the out-param of the blr at 0xdcb4dc), NOT the
     clamped per-iteration count x11. So the `uncompressed <= allocSize` check is
     against the whole run, while the copy-out length is the clamped value. Both
     of my statements were right in isolation; do not conflate the two.

CONFIRMED AS WRITTEN:
  - x22 is the remaining-sector count and IS the cbnz operand (Rt=22 in
    b5fff216); 0xdcb434 is a genuine intra-function back-edge, delta -0x1c0.
  - x21 is the output pointer (mov x21,x4 at 0xdcb418; passed as x0 to
    0xfffffff007c40550, an overlap-checking memcpy/memmove, and to
    0xfffffff007c40700, a bzero: eor x1,x1,x1).
  - The allocation argument at 0xdcb660 is x8 = (u32)[[x24+0xb0]+0x20] << 9. No
    sector-derived value reaches it. allocSize >= uncompressed length via b.ls.
  - The subtrahend at 0xdcb684 IS the value later passed as the read length: x2
    = [sp,#0x58] at 0xdcb680 is not rewritten before the blr at 0xdcb6a0.
    Cross-checked against the uncompressed sibling path, which uses the same
    vtable slot [x8+0x590] with x2 = x11 << 9 at 0xdcb534, confirming x2 is the
    length position.
  - The free at 0xdcb718 DOMINATES EVERY EXIT from the allocation path. Proven
    by building the instruction-level CFG for [0xdcb3bc,0xdcb96c) and testing
    reachability with 0xdcb718 deleted: 0xdcb6a0 (the write) -> 0xdcb5a4 NOT
    REACHABLE; 0xdcb66c -> 0xdcb5a4 NOT REACHABLE; 0xdcb66c -> 0xdcb5d4 NOT
    REACHABLE; 0xdcb66c -> 0xdcb944 (RET) NOT REACHABLE; control query with no
    deletion REACHABLE. That is a far better proof than my eyeball, and it also
    rules out a leak on those paths. Success reaches the free by fallthrough from
    0xdcb70c (mov w26,#0), joining the two error paths (cbnz w0 at 0xdcb6a8,
    read failed; cbnz w0 at 0xdcb6c4, decompress failed).
  - IOMalloc/IOFree pair confirmed structurally. 0xfffffff007b7bdf0 takes
    (size), calls 0xfffffff007684e84 with a zone/heap global at
    0xfffffff008675840, and on success does ldxr/add w9,w9,x19/stxr on the
    accounting word at 0xfffffff008779f6c. 0xfffffff007b7be48 takes (ptr,size),
    is NULL-tolerant (cbz x0 -> return), calls 0xfffffff007685134, then
    neg w8,w19 and ldxr/add/stxr on THE SAME word. Same counter, += vs -=,
    1-arg vs 2-arg, NULL-safe free: the IOLib pair with debug_iomalloc_size.

TWO NEW LEADS, both flagged by the verifier as unexplored rather than found:

 (e) *** NO BOUND CHECK ON compressedLength ANYWHERE IN THE FUNCTION. *** Every
     reference to [sp,#0x58] is add x7,sp,#0x58 (out-param, 0xdcb4d0), the ldp at
     0xdcb680 and 0xdcb768, and ldr x3 at 0xdcb6ac and 0xdcb7a0. Never a cmp.
     That is a complete reference sweep of the slot by a second party, and it
     independently confirms the shape of the defect: because dst = bufEnd -
     compressedLength, the read always ENDS at bufEnd, so the only overflow
     direction is UNDERFLOW below the buffer base when compressedLength >
     allocSize. Complements R73's "19 comparisons in read(), none involving
     [sp,#0x58]" with the dual argument - not "I counted none" but "here is
     every use, and none is a comparison."

 (f) SHIFT-WIDTH ASYMMETRY, unexplored. 0xdcb614 is `lsl w8,w8,#9` - 32-bit, so
     the result is (dbr << 9) mod 2^32 zero-extended - while 0xdcb5fc is
     `lsl x20,x9,#9`, 64-bit and untruncated, and 0xdcb618 compares them as
     64-bit. decompressBufferRequested is OUR field in the mish table, so a dbr
     >= 2^23 wraps allocSize. dbr = 0x800001 gives allocSize 512; dbr = 0x800000
     gives allocSize 0. Not obviously a new primitive on its own - the same
     allocSizes are reachable with small dbr - but it decouples allocSize from
     dbr's magnitude, which would matter if anything else ever bounds dbr. Logged
     as a lead. Do not build on it without checking reachability first.

NET: R97.4, R97.5 and R97.6 stand. Recipe O's prediction is now a derivation
backed by two independent decodes and a CFG dominance proof, with the clamp at
0xdcb4f0 supplying the advance mechanism it needs.


================================================================================
R98. *** RECIPE O IS A HIT. ONE READ REQUEST DOES ITERATE ACROSS RUNS. ***
     The kernel multiplied our magic by 24 and dereferenced it.
================================================================================

Job 702 armed Recipe O (20,188 B, CHECKPOINT PASSED, every gate green including
the two new snapshot gates on the header CRC and nEnt/eSz). the author cold-booted it.
It boot-looped several times before the chime, then on a later cycle got ~38 s in
- far enough to start the audio chain - and pop-crashed. Jobs 703 and 704 pulled
and then exported the paniclog.

R98.1  THE PANIC, DECODED.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  panic(cpu 0 caller 0xfffffff00a851b78): Kernel data abort.
    at pc 0xfffffff00ac0ef10, lr 0xfffffff00ac0ef04
  Kernel slide: 0x0000000002c00000   Kernel text base: 0xfffffff009c04000
  esr: 0x96000006   far: 0xfffffff74aa363b0
  x8:  0xfffffff74aa36298     x19: 0xfffffff051821000
  x9:  0x0000000000000018
  mach_absolute_time: 0x3637d6b2   Boot 0x96s   Calendar 0xb7s
  Panicked thread 0xfffffff0513b2000 tid 147, pid 0 kernel_task

esr 0x96000006: EC 0x25 = data abort at the same EL; IL 1; WnR bit 6 = 0, so a
LOAD; DFSC 0b000110 = translation fault level 2. An unmapped read.

Unslid (VA - 0x2c00000): pc 0xfffffff00800ef10, panic caller
0xfffffff007c51b78 (the same data-abort handler as R79). The faulting function:

  0xfffffff00800eedc  sub   sp, sp, #0x30          <- function start
  0xfffffff00800eeec  mov   x19, x0                   x19 = the object
  0xfffffff00800ef00  bl    0xfffffff00779b1dc        -> x0 = a timestamp
  0xfffffff00800ef04  ldr   w8, [x19, #0x288]      *** 32-bit INDEX from +0x288
  0xfffffff00800ef08  mov   w9, #0x18                 stride 24
  0xfffffff00800ef0c  madd  x8, x8, x9, x19           x8 = x19 + index*24
  0xfffffff00800ef10  ldr   x8, [x8, #0x118]       *** FAULT
  0xfffffff00800ef14  sub   x0, x0, x8                elapsed = now - stored

This is R80's shape again: a 32-bit field, stride 0x18, madd, dereference.

R98.2  *** THE INDEX WAS OUR MAGIC, EXACTLY. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Solving the madd backwards from the register file:

    x19 + 0x4A616371 * 0x18 = 0xfffffff74aa36298 = x8      EXACT
    x8 + 0x118              = 0xfffffff74aa363b0 = far     EXACT
    (x8 - x19) / 24         = 0x4A616371, integral, and < 2^32
    0x4A616371 LE bytes     = 71 63 61 4a = b'qcaJ'

The index the kernel read out of [x19+0x288] was 0x4A616371 - our smalloc magic,
the first word of every 16-byte tile. Two independent registers (x8 and far)
agree with the instruction's own arithmetic. A chance 32-bit match is 1 in 4.29
billion.

SO THE WRITE LANDED, AND THEREFORE THE LOOP ITERATED. READ #2 asked for 6
sectors at LBA 64. Run 1 (sectors 64-66, benign, a real stream inflating to
exactly 1536 B) supplied 3; the latch at 0xdcb5a4 subtracted 3 from x22 leaving
3; the status gate passed because run 1 returned 0; `cbnz x22` at 0xdcb5f4 took
the back-edge; and the second pass reached the poisoned run at sector 67 and
wrote 5632 bytes ending at bufEnd, i.e. from V-4096.

R97.4, R97.5 and R97.6 are now confirmed in silicon, not just decoded. And the
control is clean: Recipe N2 had the identical dbr, allocSize, zone, run geometry,
L and reach and was silent. The only variable changed was the read request's
length. That is the experiment working as designed.

R98.3  WHAT WE HIT: the Wi-Fi TimeSyncEngine.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The faulting function is in the IO80211 Wi-Fi family's time-sync code. Strings
referenced in its immediate neighbourhood:
  0xfffffff00800edc4 -> 'TimeSyncEngineState.txt'   (0x18 B before the function)
  0xfffffff00800ec3c -> 'TimeSyncEngine'
  0xfffffff00800eb38 -> 'TimeSyncEngineMessages'
  'wlan.timesync.tracebuffercount' 'wlan.timesync.sampleperiodms'
  'wlan.timesync.filterinterval'   'wlan.timesync.filtercoeff'
  'interruptTimeStamp'             'ClockUpdatePeriod(ms)'

So the victim's neighbour on this boot was a TimeSyncEngine object: 24-byte
trace records at +0x118 and the ring index at +0x288. We overwrote the index.
That also explains the ~38 s timing exactly - Wi-Fi comes up and the engine
begins sampling at its sampleperiodms cadence, which is the same moment the
audio chain starts, hence the author's "pop". The several fast pre-chime boot-loops
wrote NO paniclog (none of the 16 slots carries them), consistent with the
normal-boot console showing resets with no panic text.

Not a security-relevant structure in itself. Its value is as a measurement: it
tells us a live IO80211 object sat within 4096 bytes below a kalloc.1664 element
at probe+Wi-Fi-init time on this boot.

R98.4  MY TILE DESIGN COST US THE DISTANCE. FIX IT.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The tag greps in panicpull2.sh all returned 0, and that is not a null result -
it is a design fault in the payload. The tile is:
    [k+0]  u32 0x4A616371          <- magic, NO positional information
    [k+4]  u32 SIZE_BASE|cid<<10|k>>4
    [k+8]  u32 0x4A616371          <- magic, NO positional information
    [k+12] u32 tag<<24|cid<<20|k
Two of every four words are pure magic. The consumed field at +0x288 aligned
with one of them, so the panic proves the bytes are ours but says NOTHING about
how far below V the field sat - which is the number Step 4 actually needs.
R82.4 fixed "the ruler had nothing to say" by putting the offset in both QWORDS;
it did not put it in every WORD, and a 32-bit victim field hits a word.

FIX for Recipe P onward - 3 of 4 words positional, blind words 50% -> 25%:
    [k+0]  u32 0x4A616371                     keep ONE exact smalloc magic
    [k+4]  u32 SIZE_BASE|cid<<10|(k>>4)
    [k+8]  u32 tag<<24|cid<<20|(k & 0xFFFFF)
    [k+12] u32 0x4A610000|(k & 0xFFFF)        magic-ish high half, position low
The qword at k+0 still reads ....4A616371 for smalloc-header purposes, and the
qword at k+8 now carries tag AND position in both halves.

RULE: every 32-bit word of a payload must carry its own offset. A word that
cannot say where it came from is a wasted crash.

R98.5  TWO METHOD FAULTS OF MINE IN THIS ROUND.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 (a) `grep` on the uploaded DFU screenlog returned NOTHING for 'panic' because
     the file begins 0xFC 0x00 and GNU grep classified it as binary, suppressing
     matches silently. `grep -a` fixed it. This is the same family as R72
     (int('#0x..',0) raising), R-series (bare except swallowing it) and R97.4's
     back-edge scan (`op_str.startswith('#')` missing `cbnz x22, #..`): a tool
     that declines the input it was given WITHOUT SAYING SO. Fourth instance.
     Rule for JOB-PREFLIGHT: always `grep -a` on anything pulled off the pod or
     a serial capture, and treat a zero count from grep on a binary-ish file as
     "unanswered", never as "absent".
 (b) panicpull2.sh's register-dump section used `grep -m 4`, so it printed x0-x3
     and x28 and stopped. x4-x27 were missing - including x8 and x19, the two
     registers that solved this panic. I only got them by exporting the raw
     record with pod-get and parsing it locally. Rule: pull the raw paniclog and
     parse it off-pod; never let an on-pod grep decide what the result was.
     Also my stale-tag check reported "stale tag 0x60 : 16" - a FALSE POSITIVE,
     because the pattern 0x600 matched `cpsr: 0x60000204`. Loose hex patterns
     manufacture evidence; anchor them.

R98.6  WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ESTABLISHED: a single read request iterates across zlib runs; the per-run write
happens on the second and later passes; the victim is allocSize-sized from a dbr
of our choosing; and a live IO80211 object lay within 4096 B below it on this
boot.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and I want to be exact about this. The magic 0x4A616371 is used
by EVERY recipe from F onward, so the magic alone does not prove this record is
Recipe O's rather than a stale one. The TAG would have been conclusive and is
absent (R98.4). The attribution rests on three things instead: this record
matches no previously decoded panic (R79 was "Invalid kernel stack pointer";
R80 a data abort with x21 = 0x5a000978; R87 a spinlock timeout; R89/R92/R93
voluntary zone-integrity panics with no register dump at all); the panic
partition held ONE record replicated across all 16 slots with ~38 s uptime,
pulled minutes after the author's report; and N2, the immediately preceding boot,
produced no panic to leave behind. That is strong, and it is not the
tag-level proof I designed for. Recipe P's payload fixes this permanently.

Also still open: whether the number of loop iterations is capped. 0xdcb5d4's
`cmp w8,#0x3b` is a status ceiling and w19 (0xe00002bd) looks like an error base,
not a budget, but I have not traced every predecessor and will not claim "no
cap" on that basis. It matters before building a recipe with ~60 runs.


================================================================================
R99. NO ITERATION CAP. THE REACH IS AN UNCHECKED u64. RECIPE P ARMED.
================================================================================

R99.1  *** THERE IS NO ITERATION CAP. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Before building a recipe with many runs I had to know whether the loop is
bounded by anything other than the sector count. Scanned the whole function
[0xfffffff007dcb3bc, 0xfffffff007dcb96c), 364 instructions:

  - add/sub by #1 anywhere in the function:            ZERO
  - compares in the function:                          47, all accounted for
      0xdcb3f0-0xdcb414  entry validation
      0xdcb4ec           the clamp, cmp x8, x22 (R97.9a)
      0xdcb500-0xdcb58c  entryType dispatch: #8, #1, #1, #2, and w10 vs w9
      0xdcb5b8-0xdcb5c8  status computation
      0xdcb5d4           cmp w8, #0x3b   <- a STATUS ceiling, not a counter
      0xdcb5ec           tst x9, x10     <- status mask 0x20001
      0xdcb5f4           cbnz x22        <- THE loop condition
      0xdcb600-0xdcb644  length checks (entryType 5, uncompressed vs allocSize)
      0xdcb668-0xdcb8b0  allocation and error handling
      0xdcb958/0xdcb960  exit status mapping (tst, cmp w8 #0x54)

NOT ONE compare tests an iteration count, and there is no register or stack slot
incremented per pass. The only loop bound is x22, the remaining sector count,
decremented by the clamped consumed count. So the iteration count is OURS, set
by nEnt * eSz and the run geometry. With `mul w24,w26,w25` 32-bit, nEnt <= 0xFFFF
and eSz >= 128, a request can span ~16,383 sectors, i.e. up to ~16,383 one-sector
runs. Nothing like that is needed, but the ceiling is not the kernel's.

R99.2  THE REACH IS A FULL UNCHECKED u64 - AND A DECOUPLING QUESTION.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
compressedLength is a u64 at run-entry +0x20 (the blkx run is type u32, comment
u32, then four u64s). At the write site it is used 64-bit throughout:
    0xdcb680  ldp x2, x1, [sp,#0x58]    x2 = compressedLength (64-bit load)
    0xdcb684  sub x19, x8, x2           dst = bufEnd - x2     (64-bit sub)
    0xdcb698  mov x4, x19
    0xdcb6a0  blr [vt+0x590]            read(offset=x1, length=x2, dst=x4)
and R97.9(e)'s complete reference sweep of [sp,#0x58] found NO comparison
anywhere in the function. So dst = bufEnd - compressedLength has a full 64-bit
downward range, unchecked.

What stops that being an arbitrary-address write today is that the write LENGTH
is the same field, so reach and length are coupled: a 1 GB reach means writing
1 GB, which needs a 1 GB data fork and smashes everything in between.

*** THE OPEN QUESTION, and it is now the highest-value one on the board: does a
SHORT READ still write at the far dst? *** dst is computed from
compressedLength before the read is issued, so if the backing store supplies
fewer bytes than asked - compressedOffset + compressedLength running past the
data fork's end - and the callee copies what it got rather than failing without
writing, then reach and length DECOUPLE and we have a long-reach short-write.
That is precisely the arbitrary-address write the app-session's SS37.2 identifies
as the endgame, and it would make their one-byte AMFI gate at
0xfffffff0074ce8b1 (in __DATA_CONST, rw-) directly reachable without any text
route.
Caveats I am NOT glossing: the callee may validate the media range first and
write nothing; and even if it writes, the distance from a heap V to a static
__DATA_CONST address is not slide-derivable (their SS2), so this buys an
arbitrary write only once paired with a leak or a known relative distance. Worth
a dedicated recipe after P, and worth a static look at vt+0x590 first.

R99.3  RECIPE P - THE BANDED SWEEP. Armed as job 705, CHECKPOINT PASSED.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
recipeP1664.dmg, 45,591 B, 13 runs, merged table 724 B (kalloc.768, deliberately
a different zone from the 1664 victim). Every gate green on the live volume AND
in the snapshot the pod will boot, including the header CRC 0x2d2fbb63 and
nEnt/eSz = 96 x 128.

All runs end at bufEnd and extend downward, so ordering by DECREASING delta
layers the memory below V - a byte at depth d was last written by the last run
whose delta >= d:
    run 1  sec 64-66  delta 4096  L 5632  tag 0x70  -> band (3584, 4096]
    run 2  sec 67-69  delta 3584  L 5120  tag 0x71  -> band (3072, 3584]
    run 3  sec 70-72  delta 3072  L 4608  tag 0x72  -> band (2560, 3072]
    run 4  sec 73-75  delta 2560  L 4096  tag 0x73  -> band (2048, 2560]
    run 5  sec 76-78  delta 2048  L 3584  tag 0x74  -> band (1536, 2048]
    run 6  sec 79-81  delta 1536  L 3072  tag 0x75  -> band (1024, 1536]
    run 7  sec 82-84  delta 1024  L 2560  tag 0x76  -> band ( 512, 1024]
    run 8  sec 85-87  delta  512  L 2048  tag 0x77  -> band (   0,  512]
    alt    sec 8191   delta 4096  L 4608  tag 0x78  -> path discriminator
PLBA 64, nEnt 96 x eSz 128 = 12,288 B = 24 sectors, so READ #2 spans all eight.

Tile per R98.4, three of four words positional, encoding DISTANCE BELOW V rather
than offset-into-write so a panic register reads directly:
    [k+0]  0x4A616371                     one exact smalloc magic, kept
    [k+4]  0x3000 | j<<10 | (dist>>4)
    [k+8]  tag<<24 | j<<20 | dist
    [k+12] 0x4A610000 | (dist & 0xFFFF)
dist = delta_j - k as 20-bit two's complement:
    value <= 0x01000 -> that many bytes BELOW V
    value >= 0xFF000 -> 0x100000-value bytes ABOVE V (inside our own element)

EXPECTED AND NOT A FLAW: the decompression cache buffer is also 1536 B and is
inserted at 0xdcb6e4..0xdcb708 BEFORE the victim is freed at 0xdcb718, up to
cache-depth 5 (their SS36: not settable). Those elements are OURS, so a band
holding one will not panic. The bands that DO panic are the foreign ones, which
is the map.

R99.4  THE TWO SESSIONS' RESULTS COMPOSE. Correcting my own R97.6 overreach.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R97.6 said Step 4 "does not need a persistent groom set" and that we had been
solving the wrong problem. That was too strong, and their SS37.5 shows why.

R98 buys REPETITION AT A FIXED ADDRESS. It buys no control at all over what sits
BELOW that address - R98.3's neighbour was whatever that boot happened to park
there, a live IO80211 TimeSyncEngine object. Their 16 NVRAM OSData objects at
1664 B each (SS37.3, with the partition checksum validated 3/3 against the author's own
NOR dump in SS37.1) are exactly the lever for the other half: they decide what
the neighbours ARE.

So the correct statement is: the read loop supplies the repetition and the timed
free; the NVRAM spray supplies the occupancy. Neither replaces the other. What
R97.6 genuinely killed is only the narrower claim that the CACHE BUFFERS could
serve as the groom set (capped at 5, and predicated on an 8 KB probe read that
does not exist) - not grooming as such.


================================================================================
R100. THE RECIPE P BOOT, FROM THE UART SIDE: A NEW iBoot LINE APPEARS AFTER TWO
      FAILED BOOTS. Possible confound on every late-cycle result we have.
================================================================================

the author captured the ENTIRE cold-boot attempt for Recipe P (job 705) over UART -
five full cycles, 375 lines - and reported: silent boot-loops a few times, then
a full boot with the setup chime, then a pop restart. The panic pull is queued as
job 706. This entry is what the UART capture alone establishes, before the
paniclog arrives, because one thing in it is a methodology problem rather than a
result.

R100.1  *** A NEW iBoot LOG LINE FROM ATTEMPT 3 ONWARD. ***
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cycles 1 and 2, after the iBootStage2 banner:
    1766514c6672593:348
    3974bfd3d441da3:1045
    Delaying boot for 0 seconds. Hit enter to break into the command prompt...
Cycles 3, 4 and 5:
    1766514c6672593:348
    9905b4edc794469:694        <<< NEW
    3974bfd3d441da3:1045
    Delaying boot for 0 seconds...
    9905b4edc794469:694        <<< NEW, again
Everything else in every cycle is byte-identical.

So iBoot acquires a persistent state after two failed boots and logs it twice
per cycle thereafter. The obvious candidate is a boot-failure counter or a
breadcrumb crossing a threshold (the app-session's SS37.4 notes
`boot-breadcrumbs` as a live NVRAM variable, which iBoot maintains). The hashed
lines are filename-hash:lineno, and the hash is not invertible without knowing
the filename, so the IDENTITY of 9905b4edc794469 is NOT established - only that
it is new, persistent, and threshold-triggered.

R100.2  WHY THIS IS A CONFOUND AND NOT A CURIOSITY.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
the author's successful chime-boot came LATE in the sequence, i.e. in a cycle where the
new line was present. If iBoot takes a different path after N failures - a
fallback boot object, a different snapshot, a recovery mode - then a late cycle
is NOT the same experiment as attempt 1, and a chime-boot in cycle 4 might not
have read our image at all.

This is not hypothetical for us specifically: our arming procedure DELETES and
RECREATES the APFS snapshot under the same name every time (imgswap*.sh step 3),
so anything in iBoot that tracks boot success against snapshot state is exactly
the kind of thing that could change behaviour under us.

It also puts a question mark over earlier results that came from late cycles.
R98's panic was pulled after the author reported "boot-looped several times before the
chime, then ~38 s and a pop" - the same shape. R98's attribution rested on the
magic, the record being unlike any previous panic, and fresh timing; it did NOT
rest on knowing which cycle produced it. That attribution still stands (the magic
is ours and 1-in-4.29e9), but "which cycle" is now an open variable in every
multi-cycle boot we have recorded.

R100.3  ALSO ESTABLISHED: THE KERNEL DOES NOT LOG TO UART ON THIS BUILD.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
All five cycles run SecureROM -> iBoot stage 1 -> iBoot stage 2 -> banner ->
Delaying boot -> 13 hashed lines -> `6476b5993bf0843:102` -> silence -> reset.
`6476b5993bf0843:102` is the last line before every reset and immediately
